papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that BERT-style models encode morphological information by partitioning their embedding space into convex regions correlated with feature values, that contextualized embeddings help disambiguate ambiguous forms but not completely, and that specific attention head/layer combinations focus on subject-verb agreement.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that pre-trained BERT-style models are sensitive to morphological information, with strong performance on feature-value classification and certain attention heads learning to focus attention in a manner consistent with morphological agreement.
papers.key_findings:
BERT-style models partition their embedding space into convex sub-regions highly correlated with morphological feature value.
Contextualized embeddings allow models to distinguish ambiguous morphological forms in many, but not all cases.
Specific attention head/layer combinations hone in on subject-verb agreement.
Supervision significantly aids in extracting morphological information, as unsupervised clustering performs near random baselines.
Morphological information is best represented in the middle layers for languages with complex morphology (German and Russian), while for simpler languages it is present throughout all layers.
papers.limitation:
Models have difficulty disambiguating syncretic (ambiguous) forms, especially in languages with complex inflectional morphology.
The classification tasks require supervision; unsupervised methods (k-means) perform near random baselines.
future_direction: Identifying morphological information in BERT-style models in an unsupervised fashion.
Improving models' ability to disambiguate syncretic forms for languages with complex inflectional morphology.
Further exploration of how morphological information is shared between words via self-attention.
papers.abstract: This work describes experiments which probe the hidden representations of several BERT-style models for morphological content. The goal is to examine the extent to which discrete linguistic structure, in the form of morphological features and feature values, presents itself in the vector representations and attention distributions of pre-trained language models for five European languages. The experiments contained herein show that (i) Transformer architectures largely partition their embedding space into convex sub-regions highly correlated with morphological feature value, (ii) the contextualized nature of transformer embeddings allows models to distinguish ambiguous morphological forms in many, but not all cases, and (iii) very specific attention head/layer combinations appear to hone in on subject-verb agreement.

papers.title: Pretraining with Artificial Language: Studying Transferable Knowledge in Language Models
papers.research_question: What kind of structural knowledge learned in neural network encoders is transferable to processing natural language?
papers.core_contribution: Pretraining with an artificial language that has a nesting dependency structure provides transferable knowledge to natural language tasks, and the transferred knowledge is related to position-aware context dependence.
papers.conclusion: The transferable knowledge in pretrained encoders can be characterized as position-aware context dependence, meaning tokens in a sequence can be characterized by their neighbor tokens at specific positions.
papers.key_findings:
Pretraining with an artificial language that models statistical dependency within a sentence (Log-linear) provides a useful inductive bias for natural language modeling.
A nesting head-to-tail dependency structure is more beneficial for transfer than a flat structure.
Encoders pretrained on languages with nesting dependency structures are better at capturing local contextual information, which is important for tasks like dependency parsing.
The amount of contextual information encoded by the pretrained encoder (as measured by a probing task) correlates with its transfer performance in some cases.
The Uniform and Zipf languages, which lack token dependencies, degrade encoder performance compared to random initialization.
papers.limitation: The knowledge of position-aware context dependence may not explain every aspect of the success of cross-lingual transfer.
future_direction: Investigate how model size affects the transferability of the encoder.
Investigate if there is any difference in the knowledge transferred among different downstream tasks.
papers.abstract: We investigate what kind of structural knowledge learned in neural network encoders is transferable to processing natural language. We design artificial languages with structural properties that mimic natural language, pretrain encoders on the data, and see how much performance the encoder exhibits on downstream tasks in natural language. Our experimental results show that pretraining with an artificial language with a nesting dependency structure provides some knowledge transferable to natural language. A follow-up probing analysis indicates that its success in the transfer is related to the amount of encoded contextual information and what is transferred is the knowledge of position-aware context dependence of language. Our results provide insights into how neural network encoders process human languages and the source of cross-lingual transferability of recent multilingual language models.

papers.title: Linear Representations of Sentiment in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How is sentiment represented within Large Language Models (LLMs)? Specifically, is it represented linearly and what are the mechanisms involved?
papers.core_contribution: This paper reveals that sentiment is represented linearly in LLMs via a single direction in activation space, demonstrates its causal relevance through interventions, and discovers a 'summarization motif' where sentiment is aggregated at intermediate tokens like commas.
papers.conclusion: The work shows that sentiment is linearly represented and causally relevant in LLMs, identifies a summarization motif, and contributes to understanding internal feature representation, suggesting directions for future interpretability research.
papers.key_findings:
Sentiment is represented linearly in LLMs: a single direction in activation space captures sentiment across tasks and models.
This sentiment direction is causally relevant for sentiment tasks, as shown by activation patching and ablation experiments.
The sentiment direction generalizes across models and out-of-distribution datasets.
The model uses a circuit involving specific attention heads and neurons to process sentiment.
The summarization motif: sentiment information is aggregated at intermediate tokens without inherent valence (e.g., commas, periods), acting as information bottlenecks.
papers.limitation:
Analysis is primarily on decoder-only models, and may not generalize to other architectures.
Toy datasets are simple and may not capture full natural language complexity.
Causal interventions may not fully capture model dynamics on more complex tasks.
future_direction: Extend methods to other features beyond sentiment, such as toxicity or deception.
Investigate the summarization motif in other tasks and models.
Develop more robust methods for finding linear directions in larger models.
papers.abstract: Sentiment is a pervasive feature in natural language text, yet it is an open question how sentiment is represented within Large Language Models (LLMs). In this study, we reveal that across a range of models, sentiment is represented linearly: a single direction in activation space mostly captures the feature across a range of tasks with one extreme for positive and the other for negative. Through causal interventions, we isolate this direction and show it is causally relevant in both toy tasks and real world datasets such as Stanford Sentiment Treebank. Through this case study we model a thorough investigation of what a single direction means on a broad data distribution. We further uncover the mechanisms that involve this direction, highlighting the roles of a small subset of attention heads and neurons. Finally, we discover a phenomenon which we term the summarization motif: sentiment is not solely represented on emotionally charged words, but is additionally summarized at intermediate positions without inherent sentiment, such as punctuation and names. We show that in Stanford Sentiment Treebank zero-shot classification, 76% of above-chance classification accuracy is lost when ablating the sentiment direction, nearly half of which (36%) is due to ablating the summarized sentiment direction exclusively at comma positions.

papers.title: Large Language Models as Neurolinguistic Subjects: Discrepancy between Performance and Competence
papers.research_question: What is the distinction between performance and competence in LLMs' linguistic understanding? How do LLMs represent form and meaning across languages?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a neurolinguistic method (minimal pair probing) to assess LLMs' linguistic competence, revealing a distinction between performance and competence, and showing LLMs have stronger form competence than meaning competence.
papers.conclusion: This study adopts both psycho- and neuro-linguistic approaches to evaluating LLMs, revealing a distinction between linguistic performance and competence, and highlights the limitations of LLMs' semantic understanding.
papers.key_findings:
Psycholinguistic and neurolinguistic methods reveal that language performance and competence are distinct.
Direct probability measurement may not accurately assess linguistic competence.
Instruction tuning improves performance but does not significantly change competence.
LLMs exhibit higher competence and performance in form compared to meaning.
LLMs encode form earlier than meaning.
papers.limitation:
Limited range of languages covered in experiments.
Poor German evaluation results potentially due to very long sentences in the DistilLingEval dataset.
Experiments conducted on small-scale LLMs due to computational resource constraints.
COMPS dataset for conceptual understanding is not sufficiently fine-grained, limited to only four types of conceptual relationships.
future_direction: Include experiments covering a wider range of languages.
Construct syntactic minimal pair datasets for German.
Explore larger models to validate and extend generalizability.
papers.abstract: This study investigates the linguistic understanding of Large Language Models (LLMs) regarding signifier (form) and signified (meaning) by distinguishing two LLM assessment paradigms: psycholinguistic and neurolinguistic. Traditional psycholinguistic evaluations often reflect statistical rules that may not accurately represent LLMs' true linguistic competence. We introduce a neurolinguistic approach, utilizing a novel method that combines minimal pair and diagnostic probing to analyze activation patterns across model layers. This method allows for a detailed examination of how LLMs represent form and meaning, and whether these representations are consistent across languages. We found: (1) Psycholinguistic and neurolinguistic methods reveal that language performance and competence are distinct; (2) Direct probability measurement may not accurately assess linguistic competence; (3) Instruction tuning won't change much competence but improve performance; (4) LLMs exhibit higher competence and performance in form compared to meaning. Additionally, we introduce new conceptual minimal pair datasets for Chinese (COMPS-ZH) and German (COMPS-DE), complementing existing English datasets.

papers.title: Unveiling Instruction-Specific Neurons & Experts: An Analytical Framework for LLM's Instruction-Following Capabilities
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning reconfigure the internal computational mechanisms of LLMs to achieve superior instruction following?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the SPARCOM framework to identify and analyze instruction-specific neurons and experts, revealing how fine-tuning shapes LLMs through sparse computational components.
papers.conclusion: This study provides novel insights into how instruction tuning shapes LLMs through sparse components, demonstrating how targeted modifications to these components significantly enhance instruction-following capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Identified instruction-specific neurons (ISNs) and experts (ISEs) that are crucial for processing and executing instructions.
ISNs and ISEs exhibit both generality (overlap across instruction types) and uniqueness (high similarity within the same instruction type).
The fundamental layer-wise distribution pattern of ISNs remains largely unchanged after fine-tuning, but the number of specialized ISNs increases.
Fine-tuning significantly alters the activation patterns of ISNs for the same instruction, while the activation of experts remains highly correlated.
Proposes a three-phase mechanistic framework (early, intermediate, final) to explain the operational principles of ISNs in both dense and MoE models.
papers.limitation:
The study does not develop strategies to leverage the identified instruction-specific components to enhance the model's instruction-following capabilities and task-solving performance.
The analysis is limited to six representative instruction types, which may not capture the full diversity of instructions.
future_direction: Explore larger and more diverse datasets to identify a broader range of Instruction-Specific Neurons and Experts, enhancing the generalizability of the findings.
papers.abstract: The finetuning of Large Language Models (LLMs) has significantly advanced their instruction-following capabilities, yet the underlying computational mechanisms driving these improvements remain poorly understood. This study systematically examines how fine-tuning reconfigures LLM computations by isolating and analyzing instruction-specific sparse components, i.e., neurons in dense models and both neurons and experts in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures. In particular, we introduce HexaInst, a carefully curated and balanced instructional dataset spanning six distinct categories, and propose SPARCOM, a novel analytical framework comprising three key contributions: (1) a method for identifying these sparse components, (2) an evaluation of their functional generality and uniqueness, and (3) a systematic comparison of their alterations. Through experiments, we demonstrate functional generality, uniqueness, and the critical role of these components in instruction execution. By elucidating the relationship between fine-tuning-induced adaptations and sparse computational substrates, this work provides deeper insights into how LLMs internalize instruction-following behavior for the trustworthy LLM community.

papers.title: A gentle push funziona benissimo: making instructed models in Italian via contrastive activation steering
papers.research_question: Can activation steering be used to adapt models to Italian language tasks as an alternative to fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Activation steering can adapt models to Italian language tasks with less data and computational cost than fine-tuning, achieving comparable or better performance and higher language consistency.
papers.conclusion: Steering is a computationally cheaper alternative to fine-tuning for language adaptation, especially when using translated data, and it preserves existing knowledge without catastrophic forgetting.
papers.key_findings:
Italian steering can be successfully applied to different models, including Llama 3 and Phi 3.
Steering achieves performances comparable to or better than fine-tuned models on Italian benchmarks.
Steering yields higher quality and consistency in Italian generations compared to fine-tuning.
Steering does not suffer from catastrophic forgetting, unlike fine-tuning.
Steering is more effective on older models (e.g., Llama 2) than on newer models (e.g., Llama 3) that already have high Italian performance.
papers.limitation: Steering has a theoretical upper bound because it does not inject new knowledge into the model, only enhances existing capabilities.
future_direction: Using native examples for the steering procedure.
Exploring style-specific steering.
papers.abstract: Adapting models to a language that was only partially present in the pre-training data requires fine-tuning, which is expensive in terms of both data and computational resources. As an alternative to fine-tuning, we explore the potential of activation steering-based techniques to enhance model performance on Italian tasks. Through our experiments we show that Italian steering (i) can be successfully applied to different models, (ii) achieves performances comparable to, or even better than, fine-tuned models for Italian, and (iii) yields higher quality and consistency in Italian generations. We also discuss the utility of steering and fine-tuning in the contemporary LLM landscape where models are anyway getting high Italian performances even if not explicitly trained in this language.

papers.title: Finding Skill Neurons in Pre-trained Transformer-based Language Models
papers.research_question: How do the skills required to handle various NLP tasks distribute among the parameters of pre-trained Transformer language models? Specifically, are there specific neurons that encode these task-specific skills?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers 'skill neurons' within pre-trained Transformers—neurons whose activations on soft prompts are highly predictive of task labels—and empirically confirms these neurons encode task-specific skills, likely generated during pre-training.
papers.conclusion: The paper finds special 'skill neurons' in pre-trained Transformers that are highly predictive of task labels, confirms they encode task-specific skills, and provides evidence they originate from pre-training. It also demonstrates practical applications of this finding.
papers.key_findings:
Skill neurons generally and stably emerge across various NLP tasks and random trials.
Skill neurons are crucial for task performance, as perturbing them causes significant performance drops.
Skill neurons are task-specific, with similar tasks sharing similar skill neuron distributions.
Skill neurons are not a result of shallow word selectivity or dependent on the label words used in prompt tuning.
Skill neurons are most likely generated during pre-training rather than manufactured by the fine-tuning process of prompt tuning.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are based solely on RoBERTaBASE; it is unclear if the skill neuron phenomenon exists in other Transformer-based models.
All datasets are in English and the evaluation tasks are limited to classification, limiting linguistic and task diversity.
The analysis is limited to neurons in the feed-forward layers; other parameters like attention heads are not considered.
future_direction: Extend the skill neuron finding method to non-classification tasks and other Transformer parameters like attention heads.
Explore how skill neurons emerge during pre-training and their relationship to neurons encoding specific information found in prior work.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based pre-trained language models have demonstrated superior performance on various natural language processing tasks. However, it remains unclear how the skills required to handle these tasks distribute among model parameters. In this paper, we find that after prompt tuning for specific tasks, the activations of some neurons within pre-trained Transformers are highly predictive of the task labels. We dub these neurons skill neurons and confirm they encode task-specific skills by finding that: (1) Skill neurons are crucial for handling tasks. Performances of pre-trained Transformers on a task significantly drop when corresponding skill neurons are perturbed. (2) Skill neurons are task-specific. Similar tasks tend to have similar distributions of skill neurons. Furthermore, we demonstrate the skill neurons are most likely generated in pre-training rather than fine-tuning by showing that the skill neurons found with prompt tuning are also crucial for other fine-tuning methods freezing neuron weights, such as the adapter-based tuning and BitFit. We also explore the applications of skill neurons, including accelerating Transformers with network pruning and building better transferability indicators. These findings may promote further research on understanding Transformers. The source code can be obtained from https://github.com/THU-KEG/Skill-Neuron.

papers.title: Tuning In to Neural Encoding: Linking Human Brain and Artificial Supervised Representations of Language
papers.research_question: How does task tuning (fine-tuning vs. prompt-tuning) influence a pre-trained Transformer's neural encoding performance, and which tasks yield representations that best predict brain activity in response to Chinese language stimuli?
papers.core_contribution: Prompt-tuning produces supervised representations that predict brain activity better than fine-tuning for Chinese language neural encoding. Tasks requiring fine-grained concept and entity processing yield the most brain-predictive representations, and the proportion of tuned parameters significantly affects fine-tuning's encoding performance.
papers.conclusion: Prompt-tuning leads to better representations for predicting neural responses to Chinese stimuli compared to traditional fine-tuning on several tasks. Tasks requiring fine-grained processing of concepts and entities are most predictive of brain activation patterns, and the proportion of tuned parameters significantly influences fine-tuning's encoding performance, providing insights into the relationship between supervised ANNs and brain language representations.
papers.key_findings:
Prompt-tuning on 5 of 8 tasks yields representations that significantly exceed fully fine-tuned peers in predicting brain activities in the language network.
Tuning on tasks that require a compositional understanding of entities and concepts (e.g., Keyword Recognition and Named Entity Recognition) yields supervised representations that are better at neural encoding than tuning on other tasks.
The proportion of tuned parameters highly influences the neural encoding performance of fine-tuned models; more tuned parameters lead to worse performance for tasks where tuning decreases encoding correlation.
Prompt-tuning generally distorts pre-trained knowledge less than fine-tuning, leading to better neural encoding performance.
Only tuning on 2 of the 8 tasks (NER and KR) significantly improves neural encoding performance over the untuned model.
papers.abstract: To understand the algorithm that supports the human brain's language representation, previous research has attempted to predict neural responses to linguistic stimuli using embeddings generated by artificial neural networks (ANNs), a process known as neural encoding. However, most of these studies have focused on probing neural representations of Germanic languages, such as English, with unsupervised ANNs. In this paper, we propose to bridge the gap between human brain and supervised ANN representations of the Chinese language. Specifically, we investigate how task tuning influences a pretained Transformer for neural encoding and which tasks lead to the best encoding performances. We generate supervised representations on eight Natural Language Understanding (NLU) tasks using prompt-tuning, a technique that is seldom explored in neural encoding for language. We demonstrate that prompt-tuning yields representations that better predict neural responses to Chinese stimuli than traditional fine-tuning on four tasks. Furthermore, we discover that tasks that require a fine-grained processing of concepts and entities lead to representations that are most predictive of brain activation patterns. Additionally, we reveal that the proportion of tuned parameters highly influences the neural encoding performance of fine-tuned models. Overall, our experimental findings could help us better understand the relationship between supervised artificial and brain language representations.

papers.title: Understanding the role of FFNs in driving multilingual behaviour in LLMs
papers.research_question: How do Feed-Forward Networks (FFNs) in large language models drive multilingual behavior, and what are the patterns of multilingual processing across layers and model sizes?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the metric 'activation flatness' and analyzes FFN sublayers (detectors and combinators) to reveal distinct patterns of multilingual processing, identifying the phenomenon of 'over-layerization' where increasing layer depth without other adjustments can degrade performance.
papers.conclusion: The analysis reveals distinct patterns in FFN sublayers for multilingual processing, with detectors becoming more peaked and language-specific in later layers, and combinators showing multilingual behavior in middle layers, while also identifying over-layerization in certain model configurations.
papers.key_findings:
FFN representations are more sparse near the input and output layers across all models.
Detector activations become more peaked (less flat) through the layers, while combinator activations show a distinct drop in flatness around layer 20 regardless of model size.
Early detector layers are multilingual and process shallow features, becoming more language-specific near the output.
Combinator layers are mostly multilingual in the middle layers, with the final layers becoming language-specific, especially in larger models.
The 2.9B parameter model exhibits 'over-layerization', where increased layer depth without corresponding adjustments leads to degraded generation quality compared to the 7.5B model.
papers.limitation:
The analysis relies only on model snapshots (activations), which does not fully capture the complexities of LLMs; probing tasks or attention matrices could provide a more comprehensive understanding.
The investigation is limited to the XGLM model family, and findings may not generalize to other LLM architectures or implementations.
The analysis is limited to a set of predefined languages and test sets, which may not fully represent linguistic diversity.
future_direction: Investigate whether flatter activation patterns are easier to adapt in QLoRA fine-tuning.
Extend the analysis to more languages and explore cross-linguistic variation in more detail.
papers.abstract: Multilingualism in Large Language Models (LLMs) is an yet under-explored area. In this paper, we conduct an in-depth analysis of the multilingual capabilities of a family of a Large Language Model, examining its architecture, activation patterns, and processing mechanisms across languages. We introduce novel metrics to probe the model's multilingual behaviour at different layers and shed light on the impact of architectural choices on multilingual processing. Our findings reveal different patterns of multilinugal processing in the sublayers of Feed-Forward Networks of the models. Furthermore, we uncover the phenomenon of "over-layerization" in certain model configurations, where increasing layer depth without corresponding adjustments to other parameters may degrade model performance. Through comparisons within and across languages, we demonstrate the interplay between model architecture, layer depth, and multilingual processing capabilities of LLMs trained on multiple languages.

papers.title: BitFit: Simple Parameter-efficient Fine-tuning for Transformer-based Masked Language-models
papers.research_question: Can fine-tuning only the bias terms of a pre-trained transformer model achieve competitive performance compared to full fine-tuning, and what does this imply about the nature of the fine-tuning process?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces BitFit, a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that updates only the bias terms of transformer models, achieving competitive performance with full fine-tuning, especially for small-to-medium data, and supporting the hypothesis that fine-tuning exposes pre-existing knowledge rather than learning new task-specific knowledge.
papers.conclusion: BitFit is an effective, parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that modifies only bias terms, easing deployment and raising questions about the role of bias terms and fine-tuning dynamics in pre-trained transformers.
papers.key_findings:
BitFit, which fine-tunes only the bias terms (0.08-0.09% of parameters), achieves performance competitive with full fine-tuning on the GLUE benchmark.
For small-to-medium training data, BitFit sometimes outperforms full fine-tuning, as shown on SQuAD subsets.
Fine-tuning only a subset of bias terms (query and middle-of-MLP biases) still yields competitive results, using only 0.04% of parameters.
Randomly selecting the same number of parameters to fine-tune performs substantially worse, indicating bias terms are special for adaptation.
BitFit models exhibit a smaller generalization gap (difference between training and test error) compared to fully fine-tuned models.
future_direction: Further analysis of the role of bias terms in pre-trained networks
Investigation of fine-tuning dynamics in transformers
papers.abstract: We introduce BitFit, a sparse-finetuning method where only the bias-terms of the model (or a subset of them) are being modified. We show that with small-to-medium training data, applying BitFit on pre-trained BERT models is competitive with (and sometimes better than) fine-tuning the entire model. For larger data, the method is competitive with other sparse fine-tuning methods. Besides their practical utility, these findings are relevant for the question of understanding the commonly-used process of finetuning: they support the hypothesis that finetuning is mainly about exposing knowledge induced by language-modeling training, rather than learning new task-specific linguistic knowledge.

papers.title: LANDeRMT: Detecting and Routing Language-Aware Neurons for Selectively Finetuning LLMs to Machine Translation
papers.research_question: How to mitigate catastrophic forgetting and parameter interference when finetuning large language models for machine translation?
papers.core_contribution: LANDeRMT mitigates catastrophic forgetting and parameter interference in LLMs for machine translation by detecting language-aware neurons and selectively finetuning them, leading to improved translation quality.
papers.conclusion: LANDeRMT effectively improves translation quality and mitigates knowledge forgetting when finetuning LLMs for machine translation.
papers.key_findings:
LANDeRMT outperforms various baselines including full finetuning, adapter, and LoRA on multiple language pairs.
The method facilitates transfer learning across languages, improving performance on unseen language pairs.
Neurons are effectively categorized into language-general and language-specific based on awareness scores.
Selective finetuning of relevant neurons reduces parameter interference and catastrophic forgetting.
The conditional awareness routing mechanism dynamically allocates capacity between general and specific neurons.
papers.limitation:
Finetuning procedure may not fully overcome parameter interference as not all parameters are updated.
Computational constraints limit experiments with more training data to validate upper limits.
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in large language models (LLMs) have shown promising results in multilingual translation even with limited bilingual supervision. The major challenges are catastrophic forgetting and parameter interference for finetuning LLMs when provided parallel training data. To address these challenges, we propose LANDeRMT, a \textbf{L}anguage-\textbf{A}ware \textbf{N}euron \textbf{De}tecting and \textbf{R}outing framework that selectively finetunes LLMs to \textbf{M}achine \textbf{T}ranslation with diverse translation training data. In LANDeRMT, we evaluate the awareness of neurons to MT tasks and categorize them into language-general and language-specific neurons. This categorization enables selective parameter updates during finetuning, mitigating parameter interference and catastrophic forgetting issues. For the detected neurons, we further propose a conditional awareness-based routing mechanism to dynamically adjust language-general and language-specific capacity within LLMs, guided by translation signals. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed LANDeRMT is very effective in learning translation knowledge, significantly improving translation quality over various strong baselines for multiple language pairs.

papers.title: Birth of a Transformer: A Memory Viewpoint
papers.research_question: How do transformers balance global knowledge and in-context learning during training, specifically in the development of induction head mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a synthetic bigram dataset and an associative memory viewpoint to study learning dynamics in two-layer transformers, showing that induction heads emerge through top-down gradient-based learning.
papers.conclusion: The associative memory viewpoint provides valuable insights into transformer learning dynamics, offering a foundation for better interpretability and improvements in large language models.
papers.key_findings:
Global bigram associations are learned rapidly, while in-context induction mechanisms develop more slowly.
Transformer weight matrices can be viewed as associative memories that store input-output embedding pairs.
The induction head mechanism forms in a top-down manner, with output matrices learning before key-query matrices.
Theoretical gradient analysis shows how associative memories are recovered from noisy inputs during training.
Data distribution properties, such as trigger frequency and output uniformity, affect the learning speed and accuracy of associative memories.
papers.limitation:
The simplified transformer architecture lacks components like non-linear MLPs, multiple heads, and layer normalization, which are present in standard transformers.
The synthetic dataset may not fully capture the complexity of real-world language data.
future_direction: Extending the associative memory viewpoint to non-linear components and multi-head architectures.
Applying insights to optimization algorithms, data selection, and model editing for LLMs.
Studying how such mechanisms scale to larger models and more complex tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models based on transformers have achieved great empirical successes. However, as they are deployed more widely, there is a growing need to better understand their internal mechanisms in order to make them more reliable. These models appear to store vast amounts of knowledge from their training data, and to adapt quickly to new information provided in their context or prompt. We study how transformers balance these two types of knowledge by considering a synthetic setup where tokens are generated from either global or context-specific bigram distributions. By a careful empirical analysis of the training process on a simplified two-layer transformer, we illustrate the fast learning of global bigrams and the slower development of an "induction head" mechanism for the in-context bigrams. We highlight the role of weight matrices as associative memories, provide theoretical insights on how gradients enable their learning during training, and study the role of data-distributional properties.

papers.title: How transfer learning impacts linguistic knowledge in deep NLP models?
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning towards downstream NLP tasks impact the learned linguistic knowledge in pre-trained language models?
papers.core_contribution: Fine-tuning redistributes linguistic knowledge in pre-trained language models, with BERT retaining it deeper in the network while RoBERTa and XLNet localize it to lower layers, and the effect varies across downstream tasks.
papers.conclusion: Fine-tuning causes linguistic knowledge to be preserved in higher layers for some tasks and forgotten in others, with architectural differences: BERT retains knowledge deeper, while RoBERTa and XLNet localize it to lower layers.
papers.key_findings:
For some GLUE tasks (e.g., STS, RTE, MRPC), linguistic knowledge is preserved in higher layers after fine-tuning, while for others (e.g., SST, QNLI, MNLI) it is forgotten in higher layers.
BERT retains linguistic knowledge deeper in the network after fine-tuning, while RoBERTa and XLNet delegate it predominantly to lower layers.
Linguistic information becomes less distributed and less redundant in the network after fine-tuning, especially in RoBERTa and XLNet.
Salient linguistic neurons shift from higher to lower layers after fine-tuning in RoBERTa and XLNet.
Pruning bottom layers in RoBERTa and XLNet leads to more performance degradation than in BERT, consistent with the localization of linguistic knowledge to lower layers.
future_direction: Connecting linguistic probes with causation analysis on these tasks.
Detailed exploration of layer pruning patterns.
papers.abstract: Transfer learning from pre-trained neural language models towards downstream tasks has been a predominant theme in NLP recently. Several researchers have shown that deep NLP models learn non-trivial amount of linguistic knowledge, captured at different layers of the model. We investigate how fine-tuning towards downstream NLP tasks impacts the learned linguistic knowledge. We carry out a study across popular pre-trained models BERT, RoBERTa and XLNet using layer and neuronlevel diagnostic classifiers. We found that for some GLUE tasks, the network relies on the core linguistic information and preserve it deeper in the network, while for others it forgets. Linguistic information is distributed in the pre-trained language models but becomes localized to the lower layers post-fine-tuning, reserving higher layers for the task specific knowledge. The pattern varies across architectures, with BERT retaining linguistic information relatively deeper in the network compared to RoBERTa and XLNet, where it is predominantly delegated to the lower layers.

papers.title: Language Models Linearly Represent Sentiment
papers.research_question: How is sentiment represented within Large Language Models (LLMs)? Specifically, is sentiment represented linearly and what are the mechanisms involved?
papers.core_contribution: This paper reveals that sentiment is represented linearly in the residual stream of LLMs across multiple models and tasks, and discovers a 'summarization motif' where sentiment is summarized at intermediate tokens like commas and names.
papers.conclusion: The study concludes that sentiment is linearly represented in LLMs and identifies a summarization motif as a key mechanism for sentiment processing, providing a detailed case study for analyzing feature representation in activation space.
papers.key_findings:
Sentiment is represented linearly as a single direction in the residual stream across a range of transformer-based language models.
The sentiment direction found on simple toy datasets generalizes to real-world sentiment analysis tasks like SST and IMDB.
The sentiment direction is causally important for sentiment tasks; intervening on it can flip model predictions.
A 'summarization motif' exists: sentiment information is aggregated at intermediate tokens (e.g., commas, periods, names) without inherent valence, and this summarized information is causally relevant.
Ablating the sentiment direction at comma positions alone significantly reduces classification accuracy, demonstrating the functional importance of the summarization motif.
future_direction: Deeper investigation of the summarization motif circuitry
Exploring neurons that write to the sentiment direction further

papers.title: The Rise and Down of Babel Tower: Investigating the Evolution Process of Multilingual Code Large Language Model
papers.research_question: How do the multilingual capabilities of LLMs evolve during the pre-training process?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the Babel Tower Hypothesis to explain how LLMs evolve multilingual capabilities during pre-training, and introduces a method to optimize pre-training data distribution for multilingual code LLMs.
papers.conclusion: The Babel Tower Hypothesis explains the evolution of multilingual capabilities in LLMs, and optimizing the pre-training data distribution based on this hypothesis significantly improves multilingual performance.
papers.key_findings:
The performance of a new language during pre-training follows three stages: translation (reliance on dominant language), transition, and stabilization (use of own language-specific system).
For some languages, relying on a strong dominant language for translation is more effective than building a new knowledge system with additional data.
The internal state of the LLM, measured via working languages and language-transferring neurons, shifts from the dominant language system to the new language system over training.
Adjusting the pre-training data distribution allows different languages to reach their optimal performance state concurrently.
A method to estimate the optimal pre-training corpus distribution based on training loss and performance leads to models that outperform those trained on the original corpus.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to code languages and smaller models; future work should extend to natural languages and larger models.
future_direction: Extend the approach to natural language scenarios.
Scale to larger models.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown significant multilingual capabilities. However, the mechanisms underlying the development of these capabilities during pre-training are not well understood. In this paper, we use code LLMs as an experimental platform to explore the evolution of multilingual capabilities in LLMs during the pre-training process. Based on our observations, we propose the Babel Tower Hypothesis, which describes the entire process of LLMs acquiring new language capabilities. During the learning process, multiple languages initially share a single knowledge system dominated by the primary language and gradually develop language-specific knowledge systems. We then validate the above hypothesis by tracking the internal states of the LLMs through identifying working languages and language transferring neurons. Experimental results show that the internal state changes of the LLM are consistent with our Babel Tower Hypothesis. Building on these insights, we propose a novel method to construct an optimized pre-training corpus for multilingual code LLMs, which significantly outperforms LLMs trained on the original corpus. The proposed Babel Tower Hypothesis provides new insights into designing pre-training data distributions to achieve optimal multilingual capabilities in LLMs.

papers.title: Can you map it to English? The Role of Cross-Lingual Alignment in Multilingual Performance of LLMs
papers.research_question: How does an LLM's ability to align representations of non-English inputs to English impact its performance on NLU tasks, and does misalignment causally explain failures?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that cross-lingual alignment with English in middle layers is associated with and causally affects LLM performance on multilingual NLU tasks.
papers.conclusion: Cross-lingual semantic alignment in localized middle layers contributes causally to non-English correctness in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Transfer Success (TS) instances exhibit higher cross-lingual alignment with English than Transfer Failure (TF) instances.
Activation patching of English activations into non-English forward passes can correct incorrect predictions, indicating causal role of alignment.
Middle layers (e.g., layers 16-25) are critical for alignment and effective patching.
Control patching experiments show that semantic alignment, not just target token bias, drives corrections in specific middle layers.
Alignment peaks in middle layers and varies by language typology, with closer languages to English showing higher alignment.
papers.limitation:
Scope restricted to discriminative NLU tasks.
Benchmarks may have translation artifacts due to human translation from English.
Only analyzes bilingual alignment with English, not between other languages.
future_direction: Exploring targeted steering at inference time to leverage English activations for enhancing performance on non-English languages.
Studying potential downsides such as inflated confidence and erasure of valuable local, non-English knowledge.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can answer prompts in many languages, despite being trained predominantly on English; yet, the mechanisms driving this generalization remain poorly understood. This work asks: How does an LLM's ability to align representations of non-English inputs to English impact its performance on natural language understanding (NLU) tasks? We study the role of representation alignment in instance-level task decisions, complementing prior analyses conducted both at the language level and task-independently. We introduce the Discriminative Alignment Index ($\DALI$) to quantify instance-level alignment across 24 languages other than English and three distinct NLU tasks. Results show that incorrect NLU predictions are strongly associated with lower representation alignment with English in the model's middle layers. Through activation patching, we show that incorrect predictions in languages other than English can be fixed by patching their parallel English activations in the middle layers, thereby demonstrating the causal role of representation (mis)alignment in cross-lingual correctness.

papers.title: Enhancing Non-English Capabilities of English-Centric Large Language Models through Deep Supervision Fine-Tuning
papers.research_question: How can we enhance the non-English capabilities of English-centric large language models by explicitly supervising their internal workflow during fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a deep supervision fine-tuning method (DFT) that adds supervision to intermediate layers of LLMs to guide language conversion and English thinking, significantly improving performance on multilingual tasks.
papers.conclusion: The proposed deep supervision fine-tuning method effectively enhances the multilingual capabilities of English-dominated LLMs by guiding their internal workflow when processing non-English inputs.
papers.key_findings:
DFT outperforms traditional fine-tuning baselines on multilingual QA and NLU tasks.
DFT is more effective for QA tasks where both input and output are in the target language.
Feature-based supervision works better for understanding tasks, while logits-based supervision is more suitable for generation tasks.
Adding supervision during the English Thinking stage yields more significant improvements than during the Language Conversion stage.
An entropy-based method for selecting critical layers is preliminarily validated, though imprecise due to token variations.
papers.limitation:
The entropy-based guidance for critical layer selection is imprecise due to variations among tokens within samples.
The method is better suited for scenarios where both input and output are in the target language, rather than for cross-lingual tasks like translation.
future_direction: Further exploration of the imprecise guidance issue in entropy-based critical layer selection.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated significant progress in multilingual language understanding and generation. However, due to the imbalance in training data, their capabilities in non-English languages are limited. Recent studies revealed the English-pivot multilingual mechanism of LLMs, where LLMs implicitly convert non-English queries into English ones at the bottom layers and adopt English for thinking at the middle layers. However, due to the absence of explicit supervision for cross-lingual alignment in the intermediate layers of LLMs, the internal representations during these stages may become inaccurate. In this work, we introduce a deep supervision fine-tuning method (DFT) that incorporates additional supervision in the internal layers of the model to guide its workflow. Specifically, we introduce two training objectives on different layers of LLMs: one at the bottom layers to constrain the conversion of the target language into English, and another at the middle layers to constrain reasoning in English. To effectively achieve the guiding purpose, we designed two types of supervision signals: logits and feature, which represent a stricter constraint and a relatively more relaxed guidance. Our method guides the model to not only consider the final generated result when processing non-English inputs but also ensure the accuracy of internal representations. We conducted extensive experiments on typical English-centric large models, LLaMA-2 and Gemma-2, and the results on multiple multilingual datasets show that our method significantly outperforms traditional fine-tuning methods.

papers.title: Instruction-tuning Aligns LLMs to the Human Brain
papers.research_question: What is the effect of instruction-tuning on aligning LLM and human language processing mechanisms in terms of brain alignment and behavioral alignment?
papers.core_contribution: Instruction-tuning improves brain alignment between LLMs and the human brain, and this improvement is strongly correlated with the model's world knowledge representations.
papers.conclusion: Instruction-tuning aligns LLM representations to human brain activity, and this alignment is driven by improved world knowledge representations in the models.
papers.key_findings:
Instruction-tuning improves brain alignment by an average of 6.2% across tested LLMs.
Brain alignment is strongly correlated with model size (r=0.95) and world knowledge (r=0.81).
Instruction-tuning does not improve behavioral alignment to human reading times.
Brain alignment improvements are due to both additional training data and training to understand and follow instructions.
Smaller instruction-tuned models can achieve higher brain alignment than larger vanilla models.
papers.limitation: The BLANK2014 dataset has fewer participants (N=5) leading to greater noise in the results.
future_direction: Extend analysis to other modalities (e.g., vision, audio) and tasks (e.g., code generation, mathematical reasoning).
Study other model families and training methods.
Investigate the relationship between brain alignment and other model properties.
papers.abstract: Instruction-tuning is a widely adopted finetuning method that enables large language models (LLMs) to generate output that more closely resembles human responses. However, no studies have shown that instruction-tuning actually teaches LLMs to process language in a similar manner as humans. We investigate the effect of instruction-tuning on aligning LLM and human language processing mechanisms in two ways: (1) brain alignment, the similarity of LLM internal representations to neural activity in the human language system, and (2) behavioral alignment, the similarity of LLM and human behavior on a reading task. We assess 25 vanilla and instruction-tuned LLMs on three datasets involving humans reading naturalistic stories and sentences, and find that instruction-tuning generally enhances brain alignment (~6%), but has no similar effect on behavioral alignment. To identify factors underlying this improvement in brain alignment, we compute correlations between brain alignment and various LLM properties, such as model size, problem-solving, and world knowledge understanding. Notably, we find a strong positive correlation between brain alignment and model size (r = 0.95), as well as performance on tasks requiring world knowledge (r = 0.81). Our results demonstrate that instruction-tuning LLMs improves both world knowledge representations and brain alignment, suggesting that the mechanisms that encode world knowledge in LLMs also improve representational alignment to the human brain.

papers.title: Inspecting and Editing Knowledge Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we map natural language statements to fact encodings in an LM's internal representations to enable editing and probing of knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: REMEDI is a method that learns to map natural language statements to fact encodings in LM representations, enabling both editing of knowledge (by adding vectors to hidden representations) and probing of existing knowledge.
papers.conclusion: REMEDI links work on probing, prompting, and LM editing, and offers steps toward general tools for fine-grained inspection and control of knowledge in LMs.
papers.key_findings:
REMEDI can patch errors made by an LM and insert new facts with or without context provided in the prompt.
REMEDI can help detect errors before generation by comparing edit vectors to unedited representations.
REMEDI increases accuracy on occupation classification and factual editing tasks compared to prompting baselines.
REMEDI generalizes from out-of-context training to in-context editing, suggesting unified representation of background and contextual knowledge.
REMEDI edits preserve correlations between features (e.g., adding 'made of metal' increases probability of 'shiny').
papers.limitation:
REMEDI can occasionally lead to disfluent or incorrect generations.
REMEDI sometimes damages the essence of the entity (e.g., making Wiener schnitzel an anime instead of a food).
REMEDI can also cause unrelated facts to change (e.g., changing the air dates of a TV show).
future_direction: Developing controlled generation interfaces that allow direct steering of model behavior in representation space.
Building tools for monitoring and controlling language generation by directly specifying facts and situations in an LM's native encoding scheme.
papers.abstract: Neural language models (LMs) represent facts about the world described by text. Sometimes these facts derive from training data (in most LMs, a representation of the word "banana" encodes the fact that bananas are fruits). Sometimes facts derive from input text itself (a representation of the sentence "I poured out the bottle" encodes the fact that the bottle became empty). We describe REMEDI, a method for learning to map statements in natural language to fact encodings in an LM's internal representation system. REMEDI encodings can be used as knowledge editors: when added to LM hidden representations, they modify downstream generation to be consistent with new facts. REMEDI encodings may also be used as probes: when compared to LM representations, they reveal which properties LMs already attribute to mentioned entities, in some cases making it possible to predict when LMs will generate outputs that conflict with background knowledge or input text. REMEDI thus links work on probing, prompting, and LM editing, and offers steps toward general tools for fine-grained inspection and control of knowledge in LMs.

papers.title: Let's Focus on Neuron: Neuron-Level Supervised Fine-tuning for Large Language Model
papers.research_question: Can fine-tuning the granularity of parameter training down to the individual neuron level enable more precise and computationally efficient model updates compared to full-parameter fine-tuning and existing PEFT methods?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Neuron-Level Fine-Tuning (NeFT), a method that selectively updates individual neurons identified as sensitive to a task, achieving superior performance and efficiency compared to full-parameter fine-tuning and other PEFT methods.
papers.conclusion: NeFT is an effective fine-tuning approach that surpasses existing methods, provides insights into neuron-level dynamics during fine-tuning, and opens avenues for further optimization of neuron-level training strategies.
papers.key_findings:
NeFT outperforms full-parameter fine-tuning and other PEFT methods (like LoRA) on machine translation and summarization tasks while training a small fraction of parameters.
Neurons exhibit varying degrees of sensitivity during SFT, and selecting neurons with low cosine similarity between original and fine-tuned models is an effective strategy.
Neurons identified as sensitive for one task can be effectively transferred to similar tasks, indicating potential for transfer learning.
Training neurons with high similarity scores degrades performance and causes greater volatility in neuron utilization patterns.
Neuron selection does not require a fully converged model; neurons selected from an early training stage also deliver satisfactory results.
papers.limitation: Due to limitations of current distributed frameworks, gradient operations could only be applied to the up_proj and down_proj projections within the Llama-2-7b-chat architecture, excluding the gate_proj projections.
future_direction: Applying the NeFT method to more generation and reasoning tasks.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are composed of neurons that exhibit various behaviors and roles, which become increasingly diversified as models scale. Recent studies have revealed that not all neurons are active across different datasets, and this sparsity correlates positively with the task-specific ability, leading to advancements in model pruning and training efficiency. Traditional fine-tuning methods engage all parameters of LLMs, which is computationally expensive and may not be necessary. In contrast, Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) approaches aim to minimize the number of trainable parameters, yet they still operate at a relatively macro scale (e.g., layer-level). We introduce Neuron-Level Fine-Tuning (NeFT), a novel approach that refines the granularity of parameter training down to the individual neuron, enabling more precise and computationally efficient model updates. The experimental results show that NeFT not only exceeded the performance of full-parameter fine-tuning and PEFT but also provided insights into the analysis of neurons.

papers.title: Fine-Tuning is Subgraph Search: A New Lens on Learning Dynamics
papers.research_question: This paper investigates how fine-tuning works from a mechanistic interpretability perspective, viewing fine-tuning as a search for and optimization of a subgraph within the model's computational graph.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces circuit-tuning, a fine-tuning method that dynamically localizes and optimizes subgraphs (circuits) within a model's computational graph, enabling analysis of learning dynamics and balancing task performance with general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: Circuit-tuning provides a new method for studying learning dynamics from a mechanistic interpretability perspective, offering insights into how fine-tuning works and enabling more precise fine-tuning that balances task performance and general capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Circuit-tuning provides better training stability and preserves language modeling ability better than full fine-tuning.
The functionality of specific attention heads (Subject Attribute Heads) can reverse during fine-tuning to adapt to new tasks.
Some attention heads (Subject Identification Heads) preserve their functions and are shared before and after fine-tuning.
Nodes within a circuit cooperate through division of labor and indirect interactions to complete tasks.
Edges in the computational graph exhibit strengthening and weakening akin to Hebbian learning during fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: The study of mechanistic interpretability aims to reverse-engineer a model to explain its behaviors. While recent studies have focused on the static mechanism of a certain behavior, the learning dynamics inside a model remain to be explored. In this work, we develop a fine-tuning method for analyzing the mechanism behind learning. Inspired by the concept of intrinsic dimension, we view a model as a computational graph with redundancy for a specific task, and treat the fine-tuning process as a search for and optimization of a subgraph within this graph. Based on this hypothesis, we propose circuit-tuning, an algorithm that iteratively builds the subgraph for a specific task and updates the relevant parameters in a heuristic way. We first validate our hypothesis through a carefully designed experiment and provide a detailed analysis of the learning dynamics during fine-tuning. Subsequently, we conduct experiments on more complex tasks, demonstrating that circuit-tuning could strike a balance between the performance on the target task and the general capabilities. Our work offers a new analytical method for the dynamics of fine-tuning, provides new findings on the mechanisms behind the training process, and inspires the design of superior algorithms for the training of neural networks.

papers.title: Neuron-Level Differentiation of Memorization and Generalization in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do distinct sets of neurons underlie memorization and generalization behaviors in LLMs? Can targeted neuron-level interventions at inference time steer model behavior toward memorization or generalization? Are the observed neuron-behavior associations consistent across retraining runs and transferable across different tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that memorization and generalization activate distinct neuron subsets within LLMs, and that intervening on these subsets can controllably alter model behavior, with these neuron-behavior mappings being stable across intra-task and inter-task variations.
papers.conclusion: Memorization and generalization are encoded in separable neural pathways within LLMs, enabling inference-time steering and revealing consistent functional modularity.
papers.key_findings:
Distinct neuron subsets are responsible for memorization and generalization behaviors in LLMs.
Inference-time interventions on these neurons can steer the model's behavior toward memorization or generalization.
The neuron-behavior associations are consistent across retraining runs on the same task (intra-task consistency).
Neurons identified from one task can transfer to another task to some extent (inter-task transferability).
Behavior-associated signals originate primarily in the pretrained base model rather than the LoRA adapter.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are limited to GPT-2 and LLaMA 3.2 models, lacking validation on diverse architectures and scales.
Evaluation uses only two task types (induction-style in-context inference and arithmetic addition), not capturing the breadth of language tasks.
The operationalization of generalization is comparatively less complete than memorization, capturing only specific forms.
The inference-time intervention uses a straightforward linear neuron-shifting method, which may not be optimal.
future_direction: Broader validation on diverse architectures and scales.
Examination of more varied tasks such as QA, commonsense reasoning, or dialogue.
Development of improved neuron selection methods for higher behavioral specificity.
papers.abstract: We investigate how Large Language Models (LLMs) distinguish between memorization and generalization at the neuron level. Through carefully designed tasks, we identify distinct neuron subsets responsible for each behavior. Experiments on both a GPT-2 model trained from scratch and a pretrained LLaMA-3.2 model fine-tuned with LoRA show consistent neuron-level specialization. We further demonstrate that inference-time interventions on these neurons can steer the model's behavior toward memorization or generalization. To assess robustness, we evaluate intra-task and inter-task consistency, confirming that these neuron-behavior associations reflect generalizable patterns rather than dataset-specific artifacts. Our findings reveal modular structure in LLMs and enable controlling memorization and generalization behaviors at inference time.

papers.title: Exploring the LLM Journey from Cognition to Expression with Linear Representations
papers.research_question: How do cognitive and expressive capabilities develop and interact in large language models across pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning from human feedback stages?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that cognitive capabilities in LLMs are established during pretraining, while expressive capabilities develop during SFT and RLHF, with cognitive capability setting an upper bound for expressive capability.
papers.conclusion: This research reveals the potential connection between the hidden space and the output space, contributing valuable insights into the interpretability and controllability of LLM training processes.
papers.key_findings:
Cognitive capability is primarily established during the pretraining stage, whereas expressive capability develops during SFT and RLHF.
There is a strong statistical correlation between cognitive and expressive capabilities, with cognitive capability acting as an upper bound.
The gap between cognitive and expressive capabilities can be bridged by optimization-free methods such as few-shot learning and repeated sampling.
The vocabulary linear layer plays a crucial role in expressive capability, and its training during SFT/RLHF helps reduce the gap.
Layer-wise analysis reveals a plateau in cognitive capability in deeper layers, indicating redundancy in the model architecture.
future_direction: Exploring additional linear analysis techniques for model analysis and control.
papers.abstract: This paper presents an in-depth examination of the evolution and interplay of cognitive and expressive capabilities in large language models (LLMs), with a specific focus on Baichuan-7B and Baichuan-33B, an advanced bilingual (Chinese and English) LLM series. We define and explore the model's cognitive and expressive capabilities through linear representations across three critical phases: Pretraining, Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), and Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF). Cognitive capability is defined as the quantity and quality of information conveyed by the neuron output vectors within the network, similar to the neural signal processing in human cognition. Expressive capability is defined as the model's capability to produce word-level output. Our findings unveil a sequential development pattern, where cognitive abilities are largely established during Pretraining, whereas expressive abilities predominantly advance during SFT and RLHF. Statistical analyses confirm a significant correlation between the two capabilities, suggesting that cognitive capacity may limit expressive potential. The paper also explores the theoretical underpinnings of these divergent developmental trajectories and their connection to the LLMs' architectural design. Moreover, we evaluate various optimization-independent strategies, such as few-shot learning and repeated sampling, which bridge the gap between cognitive and expressive capabilities. This research reveals the potential connection between the hidden space and the output space, contributing valuable insights into the interpretability and controllability of their training processes.

papers.title: The Geometry of Truth: Emergent Linear Structure in Large Language Model Representations of True/False Datasets
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) linearly represent the truth or falsehood of factual statements in their internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that at sufficient scale, LLMs compute and linearly represent the truth of factual statements in their internal activations, and introduces mass-mean probing as a simple method that identifies directions more causally implicated in model outputs.
papers.conclusion: The work finds evidence that LLMs linearly represent truth at scale, localizes these representations to specific hidden states, and shows that mass-mean probing is an effective method for identifying causally implicated truth directions.
papers.key_findings:
Linear representations of truth emerge with model scale, with larger models developing a more abstract notion of truth applicable across diverse inputs.
Truth representations are localized to a small group of hidden states (over the end-of-sentence punctuation token) in the residual stream.
Simple difference-in-mean (mass-mean) probes generalize as well as other probing techniques (logistic regression, CCS) for larger models and identify directions that are more causally effective in intervention experiments.
Training probes on datasets that include statements and their logical opposites (e.g., cities and neg cities) improves generalization, mitigating the effect of non-truth correlated features.
Probes trained solely on text likelihood (the likely dataset) perform poorly on datasets where truth and probability are anti-correlated, indicating the represented feature is not merely text probability.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on simple, uncontroversial factual statements, so cannot disambiguate truth from closely related features like 'commonly believed' or 'verifiable'.
Studies only models in the LLaMA-2 family, so results may not generalize to all LLMs.
future_direction: Why were interventions with mass-mean probe directions extracted from the likely dataset effective, despite these probes being inaccurate at classification?
Why did mass-mean probing with the cities+neg_cities training data perform poorly for the 70B model, while mass-mean probing with larger_than+smaller_than performed well?
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have impressive capabilities, but are prone to outputting falsehoods. Recent work has developed techniques for inferring whether a LLM is telling the truth by training probes on the LLM's internal activations. However, this line of work is controversial, with some authors pointing out failures of these probes to generalize in basic ways, among other conceptual issues. In this work, we use high-quality datasets of simple true/false statements to study in detail the structure of LLM representations of truth, drawing on three lines of evidence: 1. Visualizations of LLM true/false statement representations, which reveal clear linear structure. 2. Transfer experiments in which probes trained on one dataset generalize to different datasets. 3. Causal evidence obtained by surgically intervening in a LLM's forward pass, causing it to treat false statements as true and vice versa. Overall, we present evidence that at sufficient scale, LLMs linearly represent the truth or falsehood of factual statements. We also show that simple difference-in-mean probes generalize as well as other probing techniques while identifying directions which are more causally implicated in model outputs.

papers.title: Semantic Pivots Enable Cross-Lingual Transfer in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How to quantify, understand, and improve the cross-lingual ability of large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a word-level cross-lingual translation task and dataset (CLWTD) to quantify cross-lingual ability, identifies co-occurrence and semantic pivot behaviors in LLMs, links them to dataset co-occurrence, and shows that constructing a semantic pivot-aware pre-training dataset improves cross-lingual ability.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes a word-level task to quantify cross-lingual ability, identifies and distinguishes two behaviors, attributes them to co-occurrence frequency, finds semantic pivots from the dataset, and improves cross-lingual ability by reconstructing a pre-training dataset.
papers.key_findings:
The Cross-Lingual Word Translation Dataset (CLWTD) provides a continuous metric that accurately reflects LLMs' cross-lingual ability.
LLMs exhibit two distinct behaviors during word translation: co-occurrence behavior and semantic pivot behavior.
These behaviors are attributed to the co-occurrence frequency of words in the pre-training dataset.
Semantic pivots can be identified from the pre-training data and show a probability trend in intermediate layers.
Constructing a pre-training dataset with a high proportion of semantic pivots effectively enhances cross-lingual ability.
papers.limitation: Due to limited availability of open-source large language models with public checkpoints and pre-training data, experiments are only validated on the OLMo-1B model.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate remarkable ability in cross-lingual tasks. Understanding how LLMs acquire this ability is crucial for their interpretability. To quantify the cross-lingual ability of LLMs accurately, we propose a Word-Level Cross-Lingual Translation Task. To find how LLMs learn cross-lingual ability, we trace the outputs of LLMs' intermediate layers in the word translation task. We identify and distinguish two distinct behaviors in the forward pass of LLMs: co-occurrence behavior and semantic pivot behavior. We attribute LLMs' two distinct behaviors to the co-occurrence frequency of words and find the semantic pivot from the pre-training dataset. Finally, to apply our findings to improve the cross-lingual ability of LLMs, we reconstruct a semantic pivot-aware pre-training dataset using documents with a high proportion of semantic pivots. Our experiments validate the effectiveness of our approach in enhancing cross-lingual ability. Our research contributes insights into the interpretability of LLMs and offers a method for improving LLMs' cross-lingual ability.

papers.title: High-Dimensional Interlingual Representations of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do multilingual large language models develop a universal interlingua representation, or present a partially aligned construct toward certain languages?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework and the Interlingual Local Overlap (ILO) metric to analyze interlingual representations in multilingual LLMs, and shows that selectively freezing early layers during single-language fine-tuning preserves interlingual alignment and improves cross-lingual generalization.
papers.conclusion: Interlingual semantic alignment is crucial for scalable multilingual learning, and the proposed framework and ILO metric provide effective tools for evaluating and preserving this alignment in multilingual LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Multilingual LLMs exhibit inconsistent cross-lingual alignments, with stronger alignment between high-resource languages and within the same linguistic family or region.
Single-language fine-tuning disrupts interlingual alignment, particularly in early layers, leading to degraded cross-lingual generalization.
Selectively freezing early layers (and other alignment-critical parameters) during single-language fine-tuning preserves interlingual alignment and significantly improves cross-lingual transfer performance.
The proposed ILO score effectively quantifies the degree of interlingual alignment by measuring the local neighborhood structure of high-dimensional representations.
Interlingual overlaps that transcend familial and regional boundaries are observed in intermediate model layers, while early and late layers show clustering by resource level and linguistic features.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) trained on massive multilingual datasets hint at the formation of interlingual constructs--a shared subspace in the representation space. However, evidence regarding this phenomenon is mixed, leaving it unclear whether these models truly develop unified interlingual representations, or present a partially aligned constructs. We explore 31 diverse languages varying on their resource-levels, typologies, and geographical regions; and find that multilingual LLMs exhibit inconsistent cross-lingual alignments. To address this, we propose an interlingual representation framework identifying both the shared interlingual semantic subspace and fragmented components, existed due to representational limitations. We introduce Interlingual Local Overlap (ILO) score to quantify interlingual alignment by comparing the local neighborhood structures of high-dimensional representations. We utilize ILO to investigate the impact of single-language fine-tuning on the interlingual representations in multilingual LLMs. Our results indicate that training exclusively on a single language disrupts the alignment in early layers, while freezing these layers preserves the alignment of interlingual representations, leading to improved cross-lingual generalization. These results validate our framework and metric for evaluating interlingual representation, and further underscore that interlingual alignment is crucial for scalable multilingual learning.

papers.title: Language Models as Artificial Learners: Investigating Crosslinguistic Influence
papers.research_question: How do L1 dominance and L2 proficiency affect crosslinguistic influence in language models, and can LMs serve as a computational framework to study human CLI?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that language models can simulate crosslinguistic influence, showing that L1 dominance and L2 proficiency predict CLI, and provides mechanistic evidence of L1 co-activation during L2 processing.
papers.conclusion: LMs can serve as artificial learners to study CLI, and the findings suggest a hybrid account where shared structures are bidirectionally primed, while non-overlapping structures are separate-but-connected and influenced by dominance.
papers.key_findings:
CLI effects are modulated by syntactic distance: similar L1 languages cause less interference or more facilitation.
Crosslinguistic priming is bidirectional for grammatical structures but sensitive to language dominance for ungrammatical structures.
LMs show preference for non-native constructions from the same L1, especially after priming.
LogitLens shows L1 token presence during L2 processing increases with L1 dominance.
L2 neuron overlap between L1 languages correlates negatively with syntactic distance.
papers.abstract: Despite the centrality of crosslinguistic influence (CLI) to bilingualism research, human studies often yield conflicting results due to inherent experimental variance. We address these inconsistencies by using language models (LMs) as controlled statistical learners to systematically simulate CLI and isolate its underlying drivers. Specifically, we study the effect of varying the L1 language dominance and the L2 language proficiency, which we manipulate by controlling the L2 age of exposure -- defined as the training step at which the L2 is introduced. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of pretraining on L1 languages with varying syntactic distance from the L2. Using cross-linguistic priming, we analyze how activating L1 structures impacts L2 processing. Our results align with evidence from psycholinguistic studies, confirming that language dominance and proficiency are strong predictors of CLI. We further find that while priming of grammatical structures is bidirectional, the priming of ungrammatical structures is sensitive to language dominance. Finally, we provide mechanistic evidence of CLI in LMs, demonstrating that the L1 is co-activated during L2 processing and directly influences the neural circuitry recruited for the L2. More broadly, our work demonstrates that LMs can serve as a computational framework to inform theories of human CLI.
