papers.title: Mechanistic Understanding and Mitigation of Language Confusion in English-Centric Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How does language confusion arise mechanistically in English-centric LLMs, and can it be mitigated through neuron-level interventions?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides the first mechanistic interpretability study of language confusion in LLMs, revealing that confusion points arise from transition failures in final layers and can be effectively mitigated by editing a small set of critical neurons identified through comparative analysis.
papers.conclusion: This work provides the first mechanistic interpretability account of language confusion in English-centric LLMs, demonstrating that targeted neuron editing can robustly mitigate confusion without sacrificing general competence or fluency.
papers.key_findings:
Confusion points are critical drivers of language confusion, and token replacement at these points reduces confusion.
Layer-wise analysis shows that language confusion is caused by failed transitions to the target language in the final layers.
Neuron-level analysis identifies specific FFN neurons in late layers that are responsible for confusion points.
Comparative importance selection of neurons enables effective mitigation of language confusion through editing.
Neuron editing achieves confusion reduction comparable to multilingual tuning for many languages while preserving general competence and output quality.
papers.limitation:
Analysis primarily focuses on the monolingual setting; cross-lingual contexts are left for future research.
Neuron editing interventions may require further validation across broader domains and model architectures.
Fully understanding how these mechanisms interact with other multilingual phenomena warrants further investigation.
future_direction: Extending analysis to cross-lingual contexts
Validating neuron editing across broader domains and model architectures
Investigating interactions with other multilingual phenomena
papers.abstract: Language confusion -- where large language models (LLMs) generate unintended languages against the user's need -- remains a critical challenge, especially for English-centric models. We present the first mechanistic interpretability (MI) study of language confusion, combining behavioral benchmarking with neuron-level analysis. Using the Language Confusion Benchmark (LCB), we show that confusion points (CPs) -- specific positions where language switches occur -- are central to this phenomenon. Through layer-wise analysis with TunedLens and targeted neuron attribution, we reveal that transition failures in the final layers drive confusion. We further demonstrate that editing a small set of critical neurons, identified via comparative analysis with a multilingual-tuned counterpart, substantially mitigates confusion while largely preserving general competence and fluency. Our approach matches multilingual alignment in confusion reduction for many languages and yields cleaner, higher-quality outputs. These findings provide new insights into the internal dynamics of LLMs and highlight neuron-level interventions as a promising direction for robust, interpretable multilingual language modeling. Code and data are available at: https://github.com/ercong21/lang_confusion.

papers.title: How Transformers Learn Causal Structure with Gradient Descent
papers.research_question: How do transformers learn causal structure with gradient descent?
papers.core_contribution: Proves that gradient descent on a two-layer transformer learns causal structure by encoding the latent causal graph in the first attention layer, with the gradient of the attention matrix encoding mutual information between tokens.
papers.conclusion: Transformers learn causal structure by encoding the causal graph in the first attention layer through gradient descent, with the gradient encoding mutual information.
papers.key_findings:
Gradient descent on a two-layer transformer learns to encode the latent causal graph in the first attention layer.
The gradient of the attention matrix encodes mutual information between tokens, and the largest entries correspond to edges in the causal graph.
For in-context Markov chains, transformers learn an induction head.
Empirically, transformers trained on the task recover a wide variety of causal structures.
For multiple parents, transformers can distribute the causal graph across multiple attention heads.
papers.abstract: The incredible success of transformers on sequence modeling tasks can be largely attributed to the self-attention mechanism, which allows information to be transferred between different parts of a sequence. Self-attention allows transformers to encode causal structure which makes them particularly suitable for sequence modeling. However, the process by which transformers learn such causal structure via gradient-based training algorithms remains poorly understood. To better understand this process, we introduce an in-context learning task that requires learning latent causal structure. We prove that gradient descent on a simplified two-layer transformer learns to solve this task by encoding the latent causal graph in the first attention layer. The key insight of our proof is that the gradient of the attention matrix encodes the mutual information between tokens. As a consequence of the data processing inequality, the largest entries of this gradient correspond to edges in the latent causal graph. As a special case, when the sequences are generated from in-context Markov chains, we prove that transformers learn an induction head (Olsson et al., 2022). We confirm our theoretical findings by showing that transformers trained on our in-context learning task are able to recover a wide variety of causal structures.

papers.title: Improving Multilingual Language Models by Aligning Representations through Steering
papers.research_question: How can multilingual alignment in LLMs be achieved efficiently by targeting a single layer through representation steering, and what does this reveal about internal structures?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a lightweight method to enhance multilingual LLMs by steering representations at a single layer, achieving performance competitive with translation systems while requiring fewer resources.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that activation-level steering is an efficient tool for improving multilingual capabilities, providing insights into internal representations and alignment.
papers.key_findings:
Single-layer steering significantly improves multilingual performance over baselines like prompt optimization and SFT.
Steering vectors can be shared across structurally similar languages, enabling zero-shot cross-linguistic transfer.
The method approaches the performance of Google Translate, with DPO steering trailing by only 3.08%.
High-resource languages dominate the representation space, and steering helps align low-resource languages.
Steering is most effective in early layers for multilingual models like Aya23, while for models like Llama2, it varies by language resource level.
papers.limitation:
probing by sweeping across all model layers is not scalable for LLMs and is impractical for real-world applications
the learnable steering vector is constrained by its fixed linear direction, limiting its capacity to capture intricate mapping relationships
experiments were focused on single layer and language, lacking multi-objective training
future_direction: Developing context-aware steering mechanisms that adapt dynamically to each prompt
Learning steering vectors by individual tokens rather than fixed vectors
Multi-objective training for simultaneous multi-language and multi-layer steering
papers.abstract: This paper investigates how Large Language Models (LLMs) represent non-English tokens -- a question that remains underexplored despite recent progress. We propose a lightweight intervention method using representation steering, where a learned vector is added to the residual stream at a single model layer to enhance multilingual performance. Through extensive experiments across seven competitive baselines -- including prompt optimization, supervised fine-tuning (SFT), in-context learning, cross-lingual transfer, and translation-based methods-we show that our approach consistently outperforms most alternatives. In particular, it achieves performance on par with production-grade translation systems while requiring far fewer resources. We further explore the complementarity between our method and SFT, demonstrating that steering offers a direct, efficient way to realign internal representations. These findings underscore the potential of activation-level interventions as a powerful tool for improving the multilingual capabilities of LLMs.

papers.title: Linearization Explains Fine-Tuning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How does linearization explain fine-tuning dynamics and performance in large language models? Specifically, how does regularization towards the pretrained model lead to linearized dynamics and how can the NTK spectrum predict fine-tuning performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that regularizing fine-tuning to remain close to the pretrained model induces linearization, allowing fine-tuning dynamics to be approximated by NTK regression, and that the NTK spectrum predicts fine-tuning performance, enabling layer selection guidance.
papers.conclusion: Linearization provides insights into fine-tuning, and the NTK spectrum can be used to predict performance and guide layer selection, saving time and computational resources.
papers.key_findings:
Regularization promotes linearity in fine-tuning, bringing the fine-tuned model closer to its linear approximation.
The condition number of the NTK correlates with fine-tuning performance, serving as an at-initialization predictor.
Layer selection affects the NTK spectrum, and spectral perturbation bounds can guide which layers to fine-tune.
The proposed linearized fine-tuning method does not sacrifice performance while providing theoretical insights.
Experiments on RoBERTa, GPT-2, and OPT-125M validate the theory across multiple datasets.
papers.limitation:
The theory applies to squared loss and gradient descent, while experiments use cross-entropy and AdamW.
The analysis is for regularized fine-tuning, and bounds for non-regularized fine-tuning are not established.
future_direction: Factor the change of σ into the layer selection methodology.
Establish bounds between non-regularized fine-tuning and linearized fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) is a popular class of techniques that strive to adapt large models in a scalable and resource-efficient manner. Yet, the mechanisms underlying their training performance and generalization remain underexplored. In this paper, we provide several insights into such fine-tuning through the lens of linearization. Fine-tuned models are often implicitly encouraged to remain close to the pretrained model. By making this explicit, using an Euclidean distance inductive bias in parameter space, we show that fine-tuning dynamics become equivalent to learning with the positive-definite neural tangent kernel (NTK). We specifically analyze how close the fully linear and the linearized fine-tuning optimizations are, based on the strength of the regularization. This allows us to be pragmatic about how good a model linearization is when fine-tuning large language models (LLMs). When linearization is a good model, our findings reveal a strong correlation between the eigenvalue spectrum of the NTK and the performance of model adaptation. Motivated by this, we give spectral perturbation bounds on the NTK induced by the choice of layers selected for fine-tuning. We empirically validate our theory on Low Rank Adaptation (LoRA) on LLMs. These insights not only characterize fine-tuning but also have the potential to enhance PEFT techniques, paving the way to better informed and more nimble adaptation in LLMs.

papers.title: Uncovering mesa-optimization algorithms in Transformers
papers.research_question: How does in-context learning emerge in autoregressive Transformers trained on next-token prediction? The paper investigates whether such training gives rise to a gradient-based optimization algorithm (mesa-optimizer) that adjusts the model as new inputs are revealed.
papers.core_contribution: Autoregressive Transformers trained on next-token prediction learn a gradient-based mesa-optimization algorithm that performs in-context learning, explaining the emergence of in-context learning and inspiring new Transformer layers.
papers.conclusion: In-context learning in autoregressive Transformers arises from mesa-optimization algorithms learned during training, which can be leveraged to design more efficient optimization-based layers.
papers.key_findings:
Early Transformer layers learn a token binding mechanism that aggregates consecutive observations into internal representations, enabling subsequent mesa-optimization.
Trained single-layer linear self-attention models implement one-step gradient descent on a least-squares objective, matching the theoretical construction.
Multi-layer linear self-attention models implement a preconditioned gradient descent algorithm that approximates the optimal least-squares solution.
The proposed mesa-layer, derived from optimization principles, performs recursive least squares and improves language modeling performance compared to standard linear attention.
Standard softmax Transformers trained on synthetic sequence tasks exhibit internal activation patterns consistent with mesa-optimization across layers.
papers.limitation: The language modeling results are not sufficient to confirm mesa-optimization in standard Transformers; more reverse-engineering is needed.
future_direction: Studying the mesa-layer equipped with forgetting factors
More reverse-engineering work to confirm mesa-optimization in standard Transformers
Designing new optimization-based Transformer layers
papers.abstract: Transformers have become the dominant model in deep learning, but the reason for their superior performance is poorly understood. Here, we hypothesize that the strong performance of Transformers stems from an architectural bias towards mesa-optimization, a learned process running within the forward pass of a model consisting of the following two steps: (i) the construction of an internal learning objective, and (ii) its corresponding solution found through optimization. To test this hypothesis, we reverse-engineer a series of autoregressive Transformers trained on simple sequence modeling tasks, uncovering underlying gradient-based mesa-optimization algorithms driving the generation of predictions. Moreover, we show that the learned forward-pass optimization algorithm can be immediately repurposed to solve supervised few-shot tasks, suggesting that mesa-optimization might underlie the in-context learning capabilities of large language models. Finally, we propose a novel self-attention layer, the mesa-layer, that explicitly and efficiently solves optimization problems specified in context. We find that this layer can lead to improved performance in synthetic and preliminary language modeling experiments, adding weight to our hypothesis that mesa-optimization is an important operation hidden within the weights of trained Transformers.

papers.title: Investigating Multilingual NMT Representations at Scale
papers.research_question: Which factors determine the extent of overlap in the learned representations? Is the extent of representational overlap similar throughout the model? How robust are multilingual NMT representations to fine-tuning on an arbitrary other language?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uses Singular Value Canonical Correlation Analysis (SVCCA) to analyze representations in a massively multilingual NMT model, revealing that encoder representations cluster by linguistic similarity, are dependent on the target language, and are robust to fine-tuning for high-resource and linguistically similar languages.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual neural networks share representations across languages strongly along the lines of linguistic similarity, and encoder representations diverge based on the target language. This work aims to inspire future research on understanding multitask and multilingual NLP models.
papers.key_findings:
Encoder representations of different languages cluster based on linguistic similarity.
Representations of a source language learned by the encoder are dependent on the target language, and vice-versa.
Representations of high resource and/or linguistically similar languages are more robust when fine-tuning on an arbitrary language pair.
Representational similarity evolves across layers, with encoder representations becoming more similar for source languages and decoder representations diverging for the target language.
The extent of distortion in representations during fine-tuning correlates with changes in BLEU scores.
future_direction: Identify and exploit the nearest neighbors of a low resource language to maximize adaptation performance.
Utilize explicit language alignment or consistency losses to enable zero-shot NMT.
Apply explicit losses, like elastic-weight consolidation, to force language representations of distant languages from getting distorted to improve transfer performance.
papers.abstract: Multilingual Neural Machine Translation (NMT) models have yielded large empirical success in transfer learning settings. However, these black-box representations are poorly understood, and their mode of transfer remains elusive. In this work, we attempt to understand massively multilingual NMT representations (with 103 languages) using Singular Value Canonical Correlation Analysis (SVCCA), a representation similarity framework that allows us to compare representations across different languages, layers and models. Our analysis validates several empirical results and long-standing intuitions, and unveils new observations regarding how representations evolve in a multilingual translation model. We draw three major conclusions from our analysis, with implications on cross-lingual transfer learning: (i) Encoder representations of different languages cluster based on linguistic similarity, (ii) Representations of a source language learned by the encoder are dependent on the target language, and vice-versa, and (iii) Representations of high resource and/or linguistically similar languages are more robust when fine-tuning on an arbitrary language pair, which is critical to determining how much cross-lingual transfer can be expected in a zero or few-shot setting. We further connect our findings with existing empirical observations in multilingual NMT and transfer learning.

papers.title: Do LLMs and VLMs Share Neurons for Inference? Evidence and Mechanisms of Cross-Modal Transfer
papers.research_question: Do LLMs and VLMs share neurons for inference? Can we leverage the mature capabilities of LLMs to enhance LVLMs at low cost?
papers.core_contribution: This work discovers a shared neuron subspace between LLMs and LVLMs and introduces SNRF, a parameter-efficient framework that transfers mature inference circuitry from LLMs to LVLMs by selectively updating shared neurons.
papers.conclusion: This work uncovers a shared neuron subspace between LLMs and LVLMs, showing that many of the most active neurons overlap across modalities and encode causal, concept-level semantics. Leveraging this insight, SNRF transfers mature textual abilities into LVLMs by selectively aligning and updating these shared neurons.
papers.key_findings:
Different series of VL models and their corresponding text-math models share a large number of neurons on inference tasks.
Shared inference basis plays an important role in a model’s performance on inference tasks.
A large portion of shared neurons are linked to math inference.
SNRF consistently improves LVLM inference performance while preserving perceptual capabilities.
Shared neurons encode consistent and interpretable concept-level effects, demonstrating their functional contribution to inference.
papers.abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) have rapidly advanced across various domains, yet they still lag behind strong text-only large language models (LLMs) on tasks that require multi-step inference and compositional decision-making. Motivated by their shared transformer architectures, we investigate whether the two model families rely on common internal computation for such inference. At the neuron level, we uncover a surprisingly large overlap: more than half of the top-activated units during multi-step inference are shared between representative LLMs and LVLMs, revealing a modality-invariant inference subspace. Through causal probing via activation amplification, we further show that these shared neurons encode consistent and interpretable concept-level effects, demonstrating their functional contribution to inference. Building on this insight, we propose Shared Neuron Low-Rank Fusion (SNRF), a parameter-efficient framework that transfers mature inference circuitry from LLMs to LVLMs. SNRF profiles cross-model activations to identify shared neurons, computes a low-rank approximation of inter-model weight differences, and injects these updates selectively within the shared-neuron subspace. This mechanism strengthens multimodal inference performance with minimal parameter changes and requires no large-scale multimodal fine-tuning. Across diverse mathematics and perception benchmarks, SNRF consistently enhances LVLM inference performance while preserving perceptual capabilities. Our results demonstrate that shared neurons form an interpretable bridge between LLMs and LVLMs, enabling low-cost transfer of inference ability into multimodal models. Our code is available at [https://github.com/chenhangcuisg-code/Do-LLMs-VLMs-Share-Neurons](https://github.com/chenhangcuisg-code/Do-LLMs-VLMs-Share-Neurons).

papers.title: Neuroplasticity and Corruption in Model Mechanisms: A Case Study Of Indirect Object Identification
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning on corrupted data change a model's internal mechanisms, and can retraining on clean data restore the original mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that fine-tuning amplifies existing circuit mechanisms, corruption localizes to specific circuit components, and models exhibit neuroplasticity by relearning original mechanisms when retrained on clean data.
papers.conclusion: The study reveals amplification, localized corruption, and neuroplasticity in model mechanisms during fine-tuning, providing insights into how models adapt and recover from poisoned data.
papers.key_findings:
Underlying mechanisms are amplified across task-specific fine-tuning, even for longer epochs.
Model corruption via toxic fine-tuning is localized to specific circuit components, altering their mechanisms rather than introducing new ones.
Models exhibit neuroplasticity, relearning original mechanisms after retraining corrupted models on clean datasets.
Amplification involves increased capacity of existing components, emergence of new components replicating prior mechanisms, and conversion of backup components to primary roles.
Corruption mechanisms differ between datasets: Name Moving disrupts Name Mover Heads and S-Inhibition Heads, while Subject Duplication alters Name Mover and Negative Name Mover Heads while suppressing S-Inhibition.
papers.limitation: The Duplication dataset corruption did not produce statistically significant changes in model mechanisms, requiring further exploration.
future_direction: Exploring more defined model poisoning attacks through fine-tuning.
Investigating the 'twinning' behavior of Name Mover and Negative Name Mover Heads in other tasks.
Further exploration of model robustness to corruption types like the Duplication dataset.
papers.abstract: Previous research has shown that fine-tuning language models on general tasks enhance their underlying mechanisms. However, the impact of fine-tuning on poisoned data and the resulting changes in these mechanisms are poorly understood. This study investigates the changes in a model's mechanisms during toxic fine-tuning and identifies the primary corruption mechanisms. We also analyze the changes after retraining a corrupted model on the original dataset and observe neuroplasticity behaviors, where the model relearns original mechanisms after fine-tuning the corrupted model. Our findings indicate that: (i) Underlying mechanisms are amplified across task-specific fine-tuning which can be generalized to longer epochs, (ii) Model corruption via toxic fine-tuning is localized to specific circuit components, (iii) Models exhibit neuroplasticity when retraining corrupted models on clean dataset, reforming the original model mechanisms.

papers.title: Finding the Translation Switch: Discovering and Exploiting the Task-Initiation Features in LLMs
papers.research_question: What internal mechanism within instruction-tuned models is responsible for the innate translation ability of LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a framework to identify 'translation initiation' features in LLMs using Sparse Autoencoders and demonstrates their causal role; proposes a mechanistic data selection strategy for efficient fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: The paper decodes the translation initiation features in LLMs and shows how mechanistic insights can be used for efficient fine-tuning and specialization.
papers.key_findings:
A small set of 'translation initiation' features are causally responsible for the model's translation ability.
Amplifying these features improves translation quality and reduces hallucinations across diverse language pairs.
These features are language-agnostic and generalize across different translation directions.
A data selection strategy that prioritizes 'mechanistically hard' samples (low activation of initiation features) improves fine-tuning efficiency and reduces hallucinations.
The identified mechanisms are transferable across scales within the same model family but not across different architectures.
papers.limitation: The translation initiation features are not transferable across different model architectures.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) frequently exhibit strong translation abilities, even without task-specific fine-tuning. However, the internal mechanisms governing this innate capability remain largely opaque. To demystify this process, we leverage Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and introduce a novel framework for identifying task-specific features. Our method first recalls features that are frequently co-activated on translation inputs and then filters them for functional coherence using a PCA-based consistency metric. This framework successfully isolates a small set of **translation initiation** features. Causal interventions demonstrate that amplifying these features steers the model towards correct translation, while ablating them induces hallucinations and off-task outputs, confirming they represent a core component of the model's innate translation competency. Moving from analysis to application, we leverage this mechanistic insight to propose a new data selection strategy for efficient fine-tuning. Specifically, we prioritize training on **mechanistically hard** samples-those that fail to naturally activate the translation initiation features. Experiments show this approach significantly improves data efficiency and suppresses hallucinations. Furthermore, we find these mechanisms are transferable to larger models of the same family. Our work not only decodes a core component of the translation mechanism in LLMs but also provides a blueprint for using internal model mechanism to create more robust and efficient models. The codes are available at https://github.com/flamewei123/AAAI26-translation-Initiation-Features.

papers.title: Universal Neurons in GPT-2: Emergence, Persistence, and Functional Impact
papers.research_question: Do models independently trained on the same task converge on similar internal structures (the universality hypothesis)? Specifically, when do universal neurons emerge, how stable are they over training, and what is their functional role?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that universal neurons (neurons with correlated activations across independently trained models) emerge early in training, persist especially in early and deeper layers, and are causally important for model predictions.
papers.conclusion: Universal neurons are functionally significant and persistent across training, especially in early and later layers, supporting the hypothesis that stable and universal representational structures emerge during language model training.
papers.key_findings:
Universal neurons emerge early in training and their proportion increases steadily, particularly in earlier layers.
Universal neurons are highly stable over time, with persistence rates near or above 80% in early and later layers, while middle layers show more volatility.
Ablating universal neurons significantly increases model loss, demonstrating their causal importance to predictions.
Ablating universal neurons in the first layer causes a disproportionately large increase in loss compared to deeper layers.
The trends of emergence, persistence, and functional impact are robust to adjustments in the correlation threshold used to define universality.
papers.limitation:
Only studied small models of a few hundred million parameters.
Monitored activations from a data subset of 5 million tokens, which is relatively small.
Only studied correlations between individual neurons as opposed to families of neurons or higher order circuits, which could offer more interpretable findings.
future_direction: Examine ablations for families of universal neurons and how the loss varies.
Monitor the effects of activation patching on some training data.
papers.abstract: We investigate the phenomenon of neuron universality in independently trained GPT-2 Small models, examining these universal neurons-neurons with consistently correlated activations across models-emerge and evolve throughout training. By analyzing five GPT-2 models at five checkpoints, we identify universal neurons through pairwise correlation analysis of activations over a dataset of 5 million tokens. Ablation experiments reveal significant functional impacts of universal neurons on model predictions, measured via cross entropy loss. Additionally, we quantify neuron persistence, demonstrating high stability of universal neurons across training checkpoints, particularly in early and deeper layers. These findings suggest stable and universal representational structures emerge during language model training.

papers.title: Emergence and Localisation of Semantic Role Circuits in LLMs
papers.research_question: Whether and how LLMs develop causally functional representations of semantic roles, specifically focusing on the localization, emergence dynamics, and cross-scale/cross-family generalization of semantic-role circuits.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces COMPASS, a causal-temporal method for discovering and tracking semantic-role circuits in LLMs, and finds that these circuits are highly localized, emerge via gradual refinement, and show partial transfer across scales and architectures.
papers.conclusion: LLMs form compact, causally isolated mechanisms for abstract semantic structure that exhibit partial transfer across scales and architectures, suggesting that transformers encode predicate-argument binding via compact circuits.
papers.key_findings:
Semantic-role information is encoded in compact, role-specific circuits (89–92% attribution within ≤20 nodes).
These circuits emerge via continuous refinement rather than discrete phase transitions.
There is a structure-function dissociation: circuits stabilize structurally before becoming functionally indispensable.
Cross-scale and cross-family analysis shows moderate component reuse (24–51% node overlap) but divergent wiring.
Larger models reuse similar components while rewiring connections.
papers.abstract: Despite displaying semantic competence, large language models' internal mechanisms that ground abstract semantic structure remain insufficiently characterised. We propose a method integrating role-cross minimal pairs, temporal emergence analysis, and cross-model comparison to study how LLMs implement semantic roles. Our analysis uncovers: (i) highly concentrated circuits (89-94% attribution within 28 nodes); (ii) gradual structural refinement rather than phase transitions, with larger models sometimes bypassing localised circuits; and (iii) moderate cross-scale conservation (24-59% component overlap) alongside high spectral similarity. These findings suggest that LLMs form compact, causally isolated mechanisms for abstract semantic structure, and these mechanisms exhibit partial transfer across scales and architectures.

papers.title: Distilled Circuits: A Mechanistic Study of Internal Restructuring in Knowledge Distillation
papers.research_question: How does knowledge distillation restructure internal circuits and representations in student models, and how can functional alignment between teacher and student be quantified?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a mechanistic understanding of how knowledge distillation restructures internal circuits, showing that students compress and discard teacher components, and introduces an alignment metric to quantify functional alignment beyond output similarity.
papers.conclusion: While student models preserve broad functional behavior from their teachers, knowledge distillation causes significant internal circuit restructuring, leading to increased reliance on fewer components and reduced robustness. The alignment metric captures functional similarity beyond output behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Student models reorganize, compress, and discard teacher components, leading to stronger reliance on fewer components.
Student models are more vulnerable to component ablation, indicating reduced robustness.
The introduced alignment metric effectively quantifies functional alignment between teacher and student models.
These findings on internal restructuring and reduced robustness generalize across different model architectures (GPT2, BERT, Llama).
Performance similarity does not guarantee similarity in internal computation; circuit-level analysis is essential for understanding functional alignment.
papers.limitation:
The study is constrained by the relatively small set of models evaluated (6).
The component role attribution procedure is manual and could be automated.
The alignment metric could be improved in granularity and interpretability.
The findings are based on specific tasks and models and may not generalize to all settings.
future_direction: Apply the methodology and alignment metric to a broader, more diverse collection of models.
Automate the component role attribution procedure, potentially using interpretability agents.
Improve the alignment metric's granularity and interpretability, and explore incorporating it as a loss term during distillation.
papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses a larger neural model (teacher) into smaller, faster student models by training them to match teacher outputs. However, the internal computational transformations that occur during this process remain poorly understood. We apply techniques from mechanistic interpretability to analyze how internal circuits, representations, and activation patterns differ between teacher and student. Focusing on GPT2-small and its distilled counterpart DistilGPT2, we find that student models reorganize, compress, and discard teacher components, often resulting in stronger reliance on fewer individual components. To quantify functional alignment beyond output similarity, we introduce an alignment metric based on influence-weighted component similarity, validated across multiple tasks. Our findings reveal that while knowledge distillation preserves broad functional behaviors, it also causes significant shifts in internal computation, with important implications for the robustness and generalization capacity of distilled models.

papers.title: Triple Phase Transitions: Understanding the Learning Dynamics of Large Language Models from a Neuroscience Perspective
papers.research_question: How do phase transitions in large language model training manifest in terms of alignment with human brain activity, internal representations, and downstream task performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies three common phase transitions in LLM training: an initial alignment with the brain when instruction following emerges, a detachment during task performance stagnation, and a realignment when tasks are consolidated.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that LLM learning involves three phase transitions that synchronize brain alignment, internal representations, and task performance, providing a multi-scale view of emergent abilities.
papers.key_findings:
Phase 1 (Brain Alignment and Instruction Following): Alignment with the entire brain surges as LLMs begin adhering to task instructions.
Phase 2 (Brain Detachment and Stagnation): LLMs diverge from the brain during a period of downstream task accuracy stagnation.
Phase 3 (Brain Realignment and Consolidation): Alignment with the brain reoccurs as LLMs become capable of solving downstream tasks.
These three phase transitions are observed across LLMs with distinct architectures and training data.
The transitions only occur when the input language matches a language sufficiently represented in the model's training corpus.
papers.limitation: The brain encoding accuracy and intrinsic dimensionality are not perfectly congruent, leaving open questions about what aspects of activation changes are not captured by intrinsic dimensionality alone.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often exhibit abrupt emergent behavior, whereby new abilities arise at certain points during their training. This phenomenon, commonly referred to as a ''phase transition'', remains poorly understood. In this study, we conduct an integrative analysis of such phase transitions by examining three interconnected perspectives: the similarity between LLMs and the human brain, the internal states of LLMs, and downstream task performance. We propose a novel interpretation for the learning dynamics of LLMs that vary in both training data and architecture, revealing that three phase transitions commonly emerge across these models during training: (1) alignment with the entire brain surges as LLMs begin adhering to task instructions Brain Alignment and Instruction Following, (2) unexpectedly, LLMs diverge from the brain during a period in which downstream task accuracy temporarily stagnates Brain Detachment and Stagnation, and (3) alignment with the brain reoccurs as LLMs become capable of solving the downstream tasks Brain Realignment and Consolidation. These findings illuminate the underlying mechanisms of phase transitions in LLMs, while opening new avenues for interdisciplinary research bridging AI and neuroscience.

papers.title: An Empirical Study on the Transferability of Transformer Modules in Parameter-efficient Fine-tuning
papers.research_question: How do different transformer modules (e.g., attention, feedforward, LayerNorms) contribute to knowledge transfer in parameter-efficient fine-tuning, and which modules are most effective?
papers.core_contribution: Every transformer module in BERT can act as a 'winning ticket' for parameter-efficient fine-tuning, with LayerNorms being the most reliable due to their high-magnitude weights, enabling competitive performance with only a tiny fraction of parameters.
papers.conclusion: Every transformer module can be a winning ticket for parameter-efficient fine-tuning, with LayerNorms being the most reliable due to their high-magnitude weights, paving the way for efficient fine-tuning without costly sub-network search or additional parameters.
papers.key_findings:
Individual modules of BERT (Multi-head attention, Feedforward, LayerNorms) can achieve comparable performance to full fine-tuning with significantly fewer trainable parameters.
LayerNorms exhibit the highest transferability, achieving good performance with only 0.03% of all parameters.
Tuning only the two LayerNorms in a single transformer block (less than 5K parameters) can yield performance comparable to tuning all LayerNorms.
Middle-layer LayerNorms show the best transferability across tasks.
The effectiveness of LayerNorms is attributed to their high-magnitude weights (outliers); tuning only these outliers leads to competitive performance.
papers.limitation:
Computational constraints limited experiments to BERT-base and only the four smallest GLUE tasks for the single-norm and outlier tuning analyses.
The Outlier Tuning method, which fine-tunes less than 0.006% of parameters, has an upper bound on its learning capability due to the extremely small number of trainable weights.
papers.abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning has garnered lots of attention in recent studies.On this subject, we investigate the capability of different transformer modules in transferring knowledge from a pre-trained model to a downstream task. Our empirical results suggest that every transformer module is a winning ticket such that fine-tuning the specific module while the rest of the network is frozen achieves a comparable performance to the full fine-tuning case. Among different modules in LMs, LayerNorms exhibit a significant capacity for transfer learning to the extent that with only 0.003% updateable parameters in the layer-wise analysis, they can show acceptable performance on various target tasks.We argue that the performance of LayerNorms could be attributed to their high-magnitude weights compared to other components in a pre-trained model.

papers.title: Exploring the Translation Mechanism of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the crucial components and their behavioral patterns in LLM translation, and can fine-tuning these components enhance translation capability?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a framework using subspace-intervened path patching to identify sparse, specialized components crucial for LLM translation, and shows that fine-tuning these components improves translation while preserving general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: The translation mechanism in LLMs is driven by a sparse set of specialized components, and targeted intervention on these components can enhance translation performance without harming general capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Only a sparse subset of heads (less than 5%) are crucial for LLMs’ translation.
Crucial heads exhibit specialized functions (source, indicator, positional) and MLPs integrate their features into English-centric latent representations.
Fine-tuning merely 64 heads achieves performance parity with full-parameter fine-tuning.
These crucial components generalize to sentence-level translation and other tasks (mathematical reasoning).
The translation mechanism is largely established during pre-training, not fine-tuning.
papers.limitation: The analysis is primarily conducted on word-level translation, which may not fully capture the complexities of sentence-level translation.
papers.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) demonstrate remarkable success in multilingual translation, their internal core translation mechanisms, even at the fundamental word level, remain insufficiently understood. To address this critical gap, this work introduces a systematic framework for interpreting the mechanism behind LLM translation from the perspective of computational components. This paper first proposes subspace-intervened path patching for precise, fine-grained causal analysis, enabling the detection of components crucial to translation tasks and subsequently characterizing their behavioral patterns in human-interpretable terms. Comprehensive experiments reveal that translation is predominantly driven by a sparse subset of components: specialized attention heads serve critical roles in extracting source language, translation indicators, and positional features, which are then integrated and processed by specific multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) into intermediary English-centric latent representations before ultimately yielding the final translation. The significance of these findings is underscored by the empirical demonstration that targeted fine-tuning a minimal parameter subset ($<5\%$) enhances translation performance while preserving general capabilities. This result further indicates that these crucial components generalize effectively to sentence-level translation and are instrumental in elucidating more intricate translation tasks.

papers.title: Beyond Learning: A Training-Free Alternative to Model Adaptation
papers.research_question: Can internal modules of language models be transplanted to improve task-specific performance without any training, and is task-specific functionality localized within specific modules?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a training-free model adaptation method called 'model transplantation' that transfers task-specific functionality by directly replacing selected internal modules (based on activation analysis) between compatible models, demonstrating localized modular structure in language models.
papers.conclusion: Transferable computation in language models is localized within specific layers, revealing an implicit modular structure, and localized parameter replacement via transplantation can serve as a viable mechanism for model editing and capability transfer.
papers.key_findings:
Transplanting activation-selected modules can improve a target model's performance without any training, sometimes surpassing the source model's performance (over-recovery).
The optimal number of transplanted modules (K) is not monotonic; performance gains peak at intermediate scales and can diminish with larger K.
In cross-generation model pairs (Phi-3/Phi-3.5), small transplant scales are dominated by FFN modules, while attention modules become increasingly prevalent as K grows.
In base vs. instruction-tuned model pairs (Gemma-2-2B/IT), activation-based selection consistently yields attention-dominant intervention sets across different K values.
Transplantation effectiveness depends on the decoding token length and the specific model pair, indicating that transfer is selective and context-dependent.
papers.limitation:
The method requires strict architectural compatibility (identical module shapes and names) between source and target models.
Evaluation is limited to a single domain (mathematical reasoning).
future_direction: Extend transplantation to heterogeneous model pairs with architectural mismatches by developing compatibility mappings between non-identical modules.
Broaden evaluation beyond mathematical reasoning to diverse domains and tasks to better characterize when and how localized module replacement yields reliable capability transfer.
papers.abstract: Despite the continuous research and evolution of language models, they sometimes underperform previous versions. Existing approaches to overcome these challenges are resource-intensive, highlighting the need for alternatives that enable immediate action. We assume that each language model has a local module inside that is suitable for a specific function. First, this work identifies a set of modules showing consistent and local activation changes under an inference workload through activation-based analysis. Subsequently, we transplant an internal module that is properly activated for a specific task into the target model, leading to immediate and measurable functional changes without additional training or fine-tuning. To experimentally demonstrate the effectiveness of the transplant technique, we quantify the relationship between transplant strength and performance improvement under different conditions for two language models. In the cross-generation setting, we find that transplanting activation-selected modules can substantially improve the underperforming model, reaching up to twice the target baseline and achieving gap-based recovery above 100%. Moreover, in transplant experiments between a base model and its instruction-tuned counterpart, transplantation improves the underperforming model toward the stronger baseline, yielding up to about 2.33 times the target baseline with gap-based recovery reaching up to 100% in the best case. These results show that meaningful capacity transfer can be realized through the implantation of highly localized modules implied by language models. Overall, this work provides empirical evidence for task-localized modularity in language models and presents a new research area: model transplantation.

papers.title: Does BERT Understand Idioms? A Probing-Based Empirical Study of BERT Encodings of Idioms
papers.research_question: Can BERT distinguish the idiomatic usage of a potentially idiomatic expression (PIE) from its literal usage? Can BERT understand the idiomatic meaning of an idiom?
papers.core_contribution: BERT can distinguish literal and idiomatic usages of potentially idiomatic expressions with high accuracy and encodes idiomatic meaning to some extent, but contextualization affects paraphrase identification differently for idioms and general multi-word expressions.
papers.conclusion: BERT is able to detect idiomatic usages of potentially idiomatic expressions with high accuracy and encode idiomatic meaning to some extent, but the effect of contextualization for multi-word expressions and idioms requires further exploration.
papers.key_findings:
BERT can separate literal and idiomatic usages of potentially idiomatic expressions with high accuracy (around 90%).
BERT can encode the idiomatic meaning of idioms to some extent, as shown by paraphrase identification performance above random baseline.
Contextualization in BERT helps most in recognizing literal usages of PIEs.
For paraphrase identification, contextualization hurts performance for general multi-word expressions but not for idioms.
The model's classification errors tend to occur on instances with lower human annotation agreement.
future_direction: Further exploration to fully explain the different effects of contextualization for multi-word expressions and idioms.
papers.abstract: Understanding idioms is important in NLP. In this paper, we study to what extent a pretrained BERT model is able to encode the meaning of a potentially idiomatic expression (PIE) in a certain context. We make use of a few existing datasets and perform two probing tasks: PIE usage classification and idiom paraphrase identification. Our experiment results suggest that BERT indeed is able to separate the literal and idiomatic usages of a PIE with high accuracy. It is also able to encode the idiomatic meaning of a PIE to some extent.

papers.title: Incremental Sentence Processing Mechanisms in Autoregressive Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: Do LMs use syntactic features or shallow heuristics to perform incremental sentence processing? Do LMs represent only one potential interpretation, or multiple? Do LMs reanalyze or repair their initial incorrect representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals that LMs use a mix of syntactic features and heuristics for incremental sentence processing, represent multiple interpretations simultaneously, and do not re-use features from garden path processing for later disambiguation.
papers.conclusion: LMs use interpretable syntactic features alongside heuristics, hold multiple interpretations, and do not reanalyze initial representations when faced with disambiguating evidence.
papers.key_findings:
Many important features are syntax-related, but some are spurious heuristics.
LMs encode multiple interpretations simultaneously.
LMs do not repair or reanalyze initial structural predictions when given disambiguating evidence.
Features found are causally relevant and generalize to larger datasets.
Probes and feature analysis show consistency.
papers.limitation:
The operationalization of p(GP) and p(non-GP) has limitations, as measuring single next tokens may not capture full continuation probabilities.
The study is limited to garden path sentences; incremental processing in more typical partial sentences remains for future work.
future_direction: Investigating incremental sentence processing in more typical partial sentences.
Improving automated neuron/feature explanation techniques.
Developing more formal ways of describing sparse features.
papers.abstract: Michael Hanna, Aaron Mueller. Proceedings of the 2025 Conference of the Nations of the Americas Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Human Language Technologies (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2025.

papers.title: Journey to the Center of the Knowledge Neurons: Discoveries of Language-Independent Knowledge Neurons and Degenerate Knowledge Neurons
papers.research_question: How is factual knowledge stored in multilingual pre-trained language models? Specifically, are there language-independent knowledge neurons and degenerate knowledge neurons?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Architecture-adapted Multilingual Integrated Gradients (AMIG) method for precise knowledge neuron localization and discovers two novel types of neurons: language-independent knowledge neurons, which store knowledge across languages, and degenerate knowledge neurons, which provide functional overlap for robust fact storage and can be used for fact-checking.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that their AMIG method enables precise knowledge localization and reveals two types of neurons that provide insights into knowledge storage, with language-independent neurons enabling cross-lingual editing and degenerate neurons enabling fact-checking.
papers.key_findings:
AMIG localizes knowledge neurons more precisely than previous methods, especially for Chinese datasets.
Knowledge neurons in m-BERT are primarily in the final layers, while in m-GPT they are distributed across early, middle, and final layers.
Language-independent knowledge neurons are concentrated in the final one or two layers and facilitate cross-lingual knowledge editing.
Degenerate knowledge neurons exist and can help PLMs detect wrong facts, improving fact-checking performance.
The existence of degenerate knowledge neurons is not dependent on multilingualism, as they are also found in monolingual models like BERT and GPT-2.
papers.abstract: Pre-trained language models (PLMs) contain vast amounts of factual knowledge, but how the knowledge is stored in the parameters remains unclear. This paper delves into the complex task of understanding how factual knowledge is stored in multilingual PLMs, and introduces the Architecture-adapted Multilingual Integrated Gradients method, which successfully localizes knowledge neurons more precisely compared to current methods, and is more universal across various architectures and languages. Moreover, we conduct an in-depth exploration of knowledge neurons, leading to the following two important discoveries: (1) The discovery of Language-Independent Knowledge Neurons, which store factual knowledge in a form that transcends language. We design cross-lingual knowledge editing experiments, demonstrating that the PLMs can accomplish this task based on language-independent neurons; (2) The discovery of Degenerate Knowledge Neurons, a novel type of neuron showing that different knowledge neurons can store the same fact. Its property of functional overlap endows the PLMs with a robust mastery of factual knowledge. We design fact-checking experiments, proving that the degenerate knowledge neurons can help the PLMs to detect wrong facts. Experiments corroborate these findings, shedding light on the mechanisms of factual knowledge storage in multilingual PLMs, and contribute valuable insights to the field. The code is available at https://github.com/heng840/AMIG.

papers.title: Language Representation Projection: Can We Transfer Factual Knowledge across Languages in Multilingual Language Models?
papers.research_question: Can cross-lingual alignment of representation spaces enable factual knowledge transfer across languages? Specifically, can we transfer factual knowledge from English to non-English languages?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes LRP2, a parameter-free method that projects representations between languages to align representation spaces, which improves factual knowledge retrieval and transfer across languages in multilingual language models.
papers.conclusion: The paper confirms that cross-lingual alignment of representation spaces enables factual knowledge transfer across languages, and proposes LRP2 as an effective method for this transfer.
papers.key_findings:
LRP2 improves factual knowledge retrieval accuracy and cross-lingual transferability for non-English languages.
LRP2 aligns representation spaces: LIRP projects non-English representations to English-like ones, and LSRP projects them back to the non-English space.
LRP2 increases the overlap of knowledge neurons between English and non-English languages, indicating enhanced cross-lingual knowledge transfer.
Cross-lingual knowledge neurons exist in multilingual pretrained language models.
Different languages require different optimal layer configurations for the LIRP and LSRP modules, indicating varying degrees of representation alignment needed.
papers.limitation:
The effectiveness of LRP2 heavily relies on the inherent capabilities of multilingual pretrained language models.
Experiments are limited to two relatively small models due to limited compute resources.
future_direction: Investigate LRP2 on larger language models.
papers.abstract: Multilingual pretrained language models serve as repositories of multilingual factual knowledge. Nevertheless, a substantial performance gap of factual knowledge probing exists between high-resource languages and low-resource languages, suggesting limited implicit factual knowledge transfer across languages in multilingual pretrained language models. This paper investigates the feasibility of explicitly transferring relatively rich factual knowledge from English to non-English languages. To accomplish this, we propose two parameter-free Language Representation Projection modules (LRP2). The first module converts non-English representations into English-like equivalents, while the second module reverts English-like representations back into representations of the corresponding non-English language. Experimental results on the mLAMA dataset demonstrate that LRP2 significantly improves factual knowledge retrieval accuracy and facilitates knowledge transferability across diverse non-English languages. We further investigate the working mechanism of LRP2 from the perspectives of representation space and cross-lingual knowledge neuron.

papers.title: Layer-Wise Evolution of Representations in Fine-Tuned Transformers: Insights from Sparse AutoEncoders
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning alter the internal representations of transformers across different layers, and what is the progression from general to task-specific features?
papers.core_contribution: Fine-tuning in transformers causes a structured progression of features across layers, where early layers retain general linguistic representations, middle layers act as transitional zones, and later layers become highly specialized for the task.
papers.conclusion: Fine-tuning transforms transformer representations in a layer-wise manner, with increasing task-specific specialization in deeper layers, providing insights into the adaptation process.
papers.key_findings:
Early layers (e.g., Layer 3) retain general linguistic representations but incorporate domain-specific features after fine-tuning.
Middle layers (e.g., Layer 6) encode a mix of general and task-specific features, shifting focus to structural tokens like punctuation after fine-tuning.
Late layers (e.g., Layer 12) become highly specialized for the task after fine-tuning, with clear differentiation based on task requirements such as sentiment polarity.
Cosine similarity analysis shows decreasing similarity between pre-trained and fine-tuned activations from early to late layers, indicating greater transformation in deeper layers.
Sparse AutoEncoders reveal that fine-tuning enhances task-specific feature encoding while preserving some general representations, demonstrating a layer-wise adaptation process.
future_direction: Expanding the scope to other transformer architectures and tasks, including multimodal and generative tasks.
Developing larger and more expressive Sparse AutoEncoders for better feature disentanglement.
Analyzing cases of poor task adaptation to understand failure modes in fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning pre-trained transformers is a powerful technique for enhancing the performance of base models on specific tasks. From early applications in models like BERT to fine-tuning Large Language Models (LLMs), this approach has been instrumental in adapting general-purpose architectures for specialized downstream tasks. Understanding the fine-tuning process is crucial for uncovering how transformers adapt to specific objectives, retain general representations, and acquire task-specific features. This paper explores the underlying mechanisms of fine-tuning, specifically in the BERT transformer, by analyzing activation similarity, training Sparse AutoEncoders (SAEs), and visualizing token-level activations across different layers. Based on experiments conducted across multiple datasets and BERT layers, we observe a steady progression in how features adapt to the task at hand: early layers primarily retain general representations, middle layers act as a transition between general and task-specific features, and later layers fully specialize in task adaptation. These findings provide key insights into the inner workings of fine-tuning and its impact on representation learning within transformer architectures.

papers.title: Hidden State Variability of Pretrained Language Models Can Guide Computation Reduction for Transfer Learning
papers.research_question: Can we measure how well-specialized each layer of a pretrained language model is for a downstream task without any tuning? Can we use that layer-wise task-specialty to guide computation reduction in transfer learning methods like fine-tuning and adapter-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a cheap-to-compute task-specialty metric based on hidden state variability that correlates with layer-wise probing performance, and proposes layer-selecting strategies that can reduce computation in transfer learning while matching the performance of tuning the entire model.
papers.conclusion: The hidden state variability metric effectively measures layer task-specialty and can guide layer selection to improve the computation efficiency of transfer learning methods like fine-tuning and adapter-tuning without sacrificing performance.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed hidden state variability ratio metric is highly correlated with layer-wise probing performance on GLUE tasks, indicating it measures task-specialty without requiring training.
Fine-tuning or adapter-tuning only the layers selected by the proposed strategies (based on the metric) can achieve performance comparable to tuning the entire model, while using significantly fewer layers and reducing computation cost.
The metric is robust to data imbalance and data scarcity in the downstream task dataset.
The metric is computed using averaged token hidden states, which yields more stable and trustworthy curves than using the CLS token hidden state.
The proposed strategies outperform baseline strategies that select top layers when constrained to tuning a small number of layers.
papers.limitation:
The metric only measures task specificity from the perspective of variability and might underestimate it if features have other kinds of good spatial structures with large within-class variability.
The proposed hidden state variability ratio only works for classification tasks; it is an open question how to generalize it to regression or generation tasks.
papers.abstract: While transferring a pretrained language model, common approaches conventionally attach their task-specific classifiers to the top layer and adapt all the pretrained layers. We investigate whether one could make a task-specific selection on which subset of the layers to adapt and where to place the classifier. The goal is to reduce the computation cost of transfer learning methods (e.g. fine-tuning or adapter-tuning) without sacrificing its performance.We propose to select layers based on the variability of their hidden states given a task-specific corpus. We say a layer is already "well-specialized" in a task if the within-class variability of its hidden states is low relative to the between-class variability. Our variability metric is cheap to compute and doesn't need any training or hyperparameter tuning. It is robust to data imbalance and data scarcity. Extensive experiments on the GLUE benchmark demonstrate that selecting layers based on our metric can yield significantly stronger performance than using the same number of top layers and often match the performance of fine-tuning or adapter-tuning the entire language model.

papers.title: Fine-tuned vs. Prompt-tuned Supervised Representations: Which Better Account for Brain Language Representations?
papers.research_question: Could prompt-tuning generate representations that better account for the brain’s language representations than fine-tuning? If so, what kind of NLU task leads a pre-trained model to better decode the information represented in the human brain?
papers.core_contribution: Prompt-tuning yields representations that better decode brain activity than fine-tuning, and tasks involving fine-grained concept meaning (like Word Sense Disambiguation and Co-reference Resolution) yield better brain decoding than tasks like syntactic chunking.
papers.conclusion: Prompt-tuned representations better decode brain activity than fine-tuned ones, and tasks involving fine-grained concept meaning are more effective for brain decoding. The proposed prompt-tuning-based framework helps understand the relationship between supervised artificial and brain language representations.
papers.key_findings:
Prompt-tuned representations consistently and significantly outperform fine-tuned peers in decoding accuracy on brain language and semantic networks.
Tuning on tasks dealing with fine-grained concept meaning (Word Sense Disambiguation and Co-reference Resolution) yields representations that are better at neural decoding than other tasks.
Fine-tuning distorts pre-trained features, while prompt-tuning preserves them, making prompt-tuning more cognitively consistent with the brain's multi-task learning ability.
The neural decoding performance of prompt-tuned representations can be partially explained by their correlation with the untuned model.
Representations tuned on half of the evaluated tasks do not significantly improve over the untuned model in neural decoding accuracy, suggesting that NLU benchmarks may not reflect brain mechanisms.
future_direction: Build benchmarks that assess the cognitive and biological plausibility of task-supervised models.
papers.abstract: To decipher the algorithm underlying the human brain's language representation, previous work probed brain responses to language input with pre-trained artificial neural network (ANN) models fine-tuned on NLU tasks. However, full fine-tuning generally updates the entire parametric space and distorts pre-trained features, cognitively inconsistent with the brain's robust multi-task learning ability. Prompt-tuning, in contrast, protects pre-trained weights and learns task-specific embeddings to fit a task. Could prompt-tuning generate representations that better account for the brain's language representations than fine-tuning? If so, what kind of NLU task leads a pre-trained model to better decode the information represented in the human brain? We investigate these questions by comparing prompt-tuned and fine-tuned representations in neural decoding, that is predicting the linguistic stimulus from the brain activities evoked by the stimulus. We find that on none of the 10 NLU tasks, full fine-tuning significantly outperforms prompt-tuning in neural decoding, implicating that a more brain-consistent tuning method yields representations that better correlate with brain data. Moreover, we identify that tasks dealing with fine-grained concept meaning yield representations that better decode brain activation patterns than other tasks, especially the syntactic chunking task. This indicates that our brain encodes more fine-grained concept information than shallow syntactic information when representing languages.

papers.title: Do Multilingual LLMs Think In English?
papers.research_question: Do multilingual LLMs perform key reasoning steps in a representation space closest to English, regardless of input and output languages?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual LLMs perform semantic reasoning in a representation space biased towards English, even for non-English inputs and outputs, as evidenced by logit lens analysis and more effective steering with English-derived vectors.
papers.conclusion: Semantic decisions in LLMs are predominantly made in a representation space close to English, while non-lexical words are processed in the prompt language, and this behavior varies across models.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs route lexical words through English representation space before translating to the target language, while non-lexical words are not necessarily routed through English.
Steering non-English prompts is more effective using English steering vectors than vectors derived from the target language.
Facts are encoded in similar layers across languages, but models have a propensity to answer in English.
The degree of English-routing varies with model multilingualism and size, with more multilingual models routing less through English.
The latent representation structure allows interpolation between facts expressed in different languages while maintaining correctness, indicating shared semantic representations with language-specific components.
papers.limitation:
Tokenization varies across languages, complicating cross-lingual comparisons.
Models may have language confidence and confusion, affecting analysis.
Interpretability methods like steering depend on prompt steerability and may push activations outside the expected distribution.
Alternative methods like sparse autoencoders were not explored due to computational constraints.
future_direction: Developing more robust evaluation procedures for interpretability methods.
Exploring alternative methods like sparse autoencoders for cross-lingual analysis.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have multilingual capabilities and can solve tasks across various languages. However, we show that current LLMs make key decisions in a representation space closest to English, regardless of their input and output languages. Exploring the internal representations with a logit lens for sentences in French, German, Dutch, and Mandarin, we show that the LLM first emits representations close to English for semantically-loaded words before translating them into the target language. We further show that activation steering in these LLMs is more effective when the steering vectors are computed in English rather than in the language of the inputs and outputs. This suggests that multilingual LLMs perform key reasoning steps in a representation that is heavily shaped by English in a way that is not transparent to system users.

papers.title: Unveiling Linguistic Regions in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether a core linguistic region exists within LLMs that facilitates cross-lingual alignment and generalization, whether distinct monolingual regions exist for individual languages, and how these regions affect further pre-training and can be used to mitigate catastrophic forgetting.
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers that LLMs possess a core linguistic region (about 1% of parameters) whose removal causes a complete loss of linguistic competence, and distinct monolingual regions for individual languages. It also shows that freezing the core region during further pre-training mitigates catastrophic forgetting.
papers.conclusion: The paper identifies a core region essential for multilingual alignment and generalization in LLMs, whose removal causes complete linguistic competence loss. Freezing this region during further pre-training alleviates catastrophic forgetting, providing new perspectives on LLMs' linguistic competence.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs possess a core linguistic region, and removing this region (setting parameters to zero) results in a significant loss of the model's linguistic capabilities across 30 languages.
This core region exhibits significant dimensional dependence; perturbations to specific dimensions or even a single parameter can lead to a substantial decline in linguistic ability.
Distinct monolingual regions exist in LLMs for different languages. Removing a specific monolingual region causes a significant deterioration in the linguistic capabilities within the corresponding language.
Freezing the core linguistic region during further pre-training can mitigate the issue of catastrophic forgetting, a common phenomenon observed during further pre-training of LLMs.
The core linguistic region is concentrated in specific rows and columns of the attention and feedforward layer matrices, and its removal leads to a complete loss of model proficiency.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are based on LLaMA-2-7B/13B, and it remains to be further determined whether the same phenomena are observable in larger or differently architected models.
Optimizing full-scale fine-tuning through the freezing operation is not suited to extensive datasets. A more feasible approach is to limit the magnitude of parameter updates.
future_direction: Exploring whether the same phenomena are observable in larger or differently architected models.
Using a more feasible approach of limiting the magnitude of parameter updates instead of freezing for extensive datasets.
Exploring knowledge as a higher-level semantic representation beyond language.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated considerable cross-lingual alignment and generalization ability. Current research primarily focuses on improving LLMs' cross-lingual generalization capabilities. However, there is still a lack of research on the intrinsic mechanisms of how LLMs achieve cross-lingual alignment. From the perspective of region partitioning, this paper conducts several investigations on the linguistic competence of LLMs. We discover a core region in LLMs that corresponds to linguistic competence, accounting for approximately 1% of the total model parameters. Removing this core region by setting parameters to zero results in a significant performance decrease across 30 different languages. Furthermore, this core region exhibits significant dimensional dependence, perturbations to even a single parameter on specific dimensions leading to a loss of linguistic competence. Moreover, we discover that distinct monolingual regions exist for different languages, and disruption to these specific regions substantially reduces the LLMs' proficiency in those corresponding languages. Our research also indicates that freezing the core linguistic region during further pre-training can mitigate the issue of catastrophic forgetting (CF), a common phenomenon observed during further pre-training of LLMs. Overall, exploring the LLMs' functional regions provides insights into the foundation of their intelligence.

papers.title: Language Steering for Multilingual In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: Does language identity occupy structured directions in activation space, and can a simple activation offset improve multilingual in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces language vectors, a training-free method that improves multilingual in-context learning by steering activations, and shows that language identity occupies structured directions in activation space.
papers.conclusion: Language vectors improve multilingual in-context learning and encode meaningful linguistic structure, supporting the hypothesis that language identity occupies structured directions in activation space.
papers.key_findings:
Language vectors improve performance over baselines across tasks and languages.
Vectors encode linguistic structure, with related languages clustering together.
Vectors transfer across tasks, indicating they capture language-specific rather than task-specific information.
Steering is most effective in early to middle layers.
The method is training-free and requires no parameter updates.
papers.limitation:
Hyperparameters are selected per language via validation performance, which requires held-out data and may not generalize to new languages or domains.
Evaluation is limited to instruction-tuned decoder-only models.
Certain task transfers fail (e.g., MSVAMP to XNLI).
future_direction: Extending the approach to languages without parallel data.
Applying language vectors to generative tasks such as summarization.
Predicting steering effectiveness without exhaustive hyperparameter search.
papers.abstract: While multilingual large language models have gained widespread adoption, their performance on non-English languages remains substantially inferior to English. This disparity is particularly evident in in-context learning scenarios, where providing demonstrations in English but testing on non-English inputs leads to significant performance degradation. In this paper, we hypothesize that LLMs develop a universal semantic space for understanding languages, where different languages are encoded as distinct directions within this space. Based on this hypothesis, we propose language vectors -- a training-free language steering approach that leverages activation differences between source and target languages to guide model behavior. We steer the model generations by adding the vector to the intermediate model activations during inference. This is done to make the model's internal representations shift towards the target language space without any parameter updates. We evaluate our method across three datasets and test on a total of 19 languages on three different models. Our results show consistent improvements on multilingual in-context learning over baselines across all tasks and languages tested. Beyond performance gains, hierarchical clustering of steering vectors reveals meaningful linguistic structure aligned with language families. These vectors also successfully transfer across tasks, demonstrating that these representations are task-agnostic.

papers.title: Unveiling Language Competence Neurons: A Psycholinguistic Approach to Model Interpretability
